# Weekly report

This example schedules a report for Monday at 09:00 in Africa/Kampala. The job counts the tasks in the starter's table, builds a report and passes it to a queue. The queue writes the report to an `outbox` folder, which stands in for email. You will also run the job on demand, which is how you test a schedule before it fires.

## What you need [#what-you-need]

- The starter project from the [examples overview](/guide/examples), installed with `bun install`.
- Stop `bun run dev` before running the on-demand script. Both start a server on port 8000.

## 1. Add the logger module [#1-add-the-logger-module]

Create `src/observability.ts`. The schedule and the queue share this logger:

```ts
import { createLogger } from "@nilejs/nile";

export const logger = createLogger("my-app", {
  mode: "dev",
  chunking: "monthly",
});
```

## 2. Write the job and the queue [#2-write-the-job-and-the-queue]

Create `src/reports/weekly-report.ts`. It has four parts: the report builder, a queue with one worker, the job that connects them, and the schedule that runs the job every Monday:

```ts
import { type JobRunContext, type JobRunEvent, type SchedulerOptions, utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok, type Result } from "slang-ts";
import { taskModel } from "@/db/models";
import { logger } from "@/observability";

export interface WeeklyReport {
  name: string;
  generatedAt: string;
  totalTasks: number;
  pendingTasks: number;
  doneTasks: number;
}

export interface DeliveryResult {
  path: string;
}

const OUTBOX_DIRECTORY = "outbox";

/** Writes the report to the outbox folder. Replace this with an email or storage call. */
const deliverReport = async (
  report: WeeklyReport,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<Result<DeliveryResult, string>> => {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    return Err("Delivery was cancelled");
  }

  const path = `${OUTBOX_DIRECTORY}/${report.name}.json`;
  await Bun.write(path, JSON.stringify(report, null, 2));
  return Ok({ path: path });
};

/** One delivery at a time keeps the outbox writes in order. */
export const reportQueue = utils.createQueue<WeeklyReport, DeliveryResult>({
  task: deliverReport,
  concurrency: 1,
  capacity: 100,
});

const buildWeeklyReport = async (generatedAt: Date): Promise<Result<WeeklyReport, string>> => {
  const tasks = await taskModel.findAll();
  if (tasks.isErr) {
    return Err(tasks.error);
  }

  const rows = tasks.value;
  const doneTasks = rows.filter((task) => task.status === "done").length;
  const pendingTasks = rows.filter((task) => task.status === "pending").length;

  return Ok({
    name: `weekly-${generatedAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`,
    generatedAt: generatedAt.toISOString(),
    totalTasks: rows.length,
    pendingTasks: pendingTasks,
    doneTasks: doneTasks,
  });
};

/** Scheduled job: build the report, then hand delivery to the queue. */
export const weeklyReportJob = async (
  run: JobRunContext
): Promise<Result<{ report: string; path: string }, string>> => {
  const built = await buildWeeklyReport(run.scheduledAt);
  if (built.isErr) {
    return Err(built.error);
  }

  const delivered = await reportQueue.run(built.value, { signal: run.signal });
  if (delivered.isErr) {
    return Err(delivered.error);
  }

  return Ok({ report: built.value.name, path: delivered.value.path });
};

export const recordRunEvent = (event: JobRunEvent): void => {
  logger.info({
    atFunction: "scheduler",
    message: `Job ${event.job} ${event.phase}`,
    data: { runId: event.runId, durationMs: event.durationMs ?? null },
  });
};

export const schedules: SchedulerOptions = {
  jobs: [
    {
      name: "weekly-report",
      schedule: {
        weekly: "monday",
        at: "09:00",
        timezone: "Africa/Kampala",
      },
      handler: weeklyReportJob,
    },
  ],
  onRunEvent: recordRunEvent,
};
```

`reportQueue` allows one delivery at a time and holds up to 100 waiting reports. The job returns the Result of the delivery, so a failed write appears as a failed run.

## 3. Register the schedule [#3-register-the-schedule]

Replace `src/index.ts`. The only change from the starter is the `schedules` option and the shared logger:

```ts
import { createNileServer } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { Ok, safeTry } from "slang-ts";
import { db } from "@/db/client";
import { schedules } from "@/reports/weekly-report";
import { logger } from "@/observability";
import { services } from "@/services/services.config";

/** Push schema to PGLite on boot */
const pushSchema = async () => {
  const result = await safeTry(() =>
    db.execute(sql`
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
        title TEXT NOT NULL,
        description TEXT,
        status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
        created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
        updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
      )
    `)
  );

  if (result.isErr) {
    console.error("[pushSchema] Failed:", result.error);
  }
};

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "my-app",
  runtime: "bun",
  native: true,
  project: { structure: "error" },
  services,
  resources: { logger, database: db },
  schedules: schedules,
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    host: "localhost",
    port: 8000,
    allowedOrigins: ["http://localhost:8000"],
    enableStatus: true,
  },
  onBoot: {
    // The first PGlite start on a slow machine can take longer than the 10 second default.
    maxWaitTime: 30_000,
    fn: async (ctx) => {
      await pushSchema();
      ctx.resources?.logger?.info({
        atFunction: "onBoot",
        message: "my-app booted - PGLite schema ready",
      });
      return Ok(null);
    },
  },
});

if (server.nativeRest) {
  const port = server.config.rest?.port ?? 8000;
  Bun.serve({ port, fetch: server.nativeRest.fetch });
  console.log(`\nmy-app listening on http://localhost:${port}\n`);
}
```

## 4. Add the on-demand script [#4-add-the-on-demand-script]

Create `scripts/run-weekly-report.ts`. It starts the server, prints the schedule state, runs the job now and shuts down:

```ts
import { server } from "../src/index";

console.log("jobs:", JSON.stringify(server.scheduler?.inspect()));

const outcome = await server.scheduler?.runNow("weekly-report");
if (outcome === undefined) {
  throw new Error("Scheduler is not running");
}
console.log("runNow:", outcome.isErr ? `error: ${outcome.error}` : JSON.stringify(outcome.value));

await server.lifecycle.shutdown({ timeoutMs: 5000 });
process.exit(0);
```

## 5. Run the job now [#5-run-the-job-now]

```sh
bun run scripts/run-weekly-report.ts
```

The server starts first and prints its usual startup lines. Then the script prints the schedule and the run. The lines that matter look like this:

```text
jobs: [{"name":"weekly-report","running":true,"active":false,"nextRun":"2026-10-26T06:00:00.000Z"}]
22:31:21.350 INFO  scheduler Job weekly-report started {
  runId: "1d947f73-b935-47ac-9c77-fa29c549d650",
  durationMs: null,
}
22:31:21.367 INFO  scheduler Job weekly-report completed {
  runId: "1d947f73-b935-47ac-9c77-fa29c549d650",
  durationMs: 17.6066330000001,
}
runNow: {"report":"weekly-2026-10-22","path":"outbox/weekly-2026-10-22.json"}
```

`nextRun` is the next Monday at 09:00 in Africa/Kampala, which is 06:00 UTC. The date changes each week. The `report` name uses the scheduled date, so a run on 22 October is named `weekly-2026-10-22`.

Check the file the queue wrote:

```sh
cat outbox/weekly-*.json
```

You should see the report fields:

```json
{
  "name": "weekly-2026-10-22",
  "generatedAt": "2026-10-22T22:31:21.349Z",
  "totalTasks": 1,
  "pendingTasks": 1,
  "doneTasks": 0
}
```

The counts depend on the tasks in your database. The script creates the `outbox` folder when it writes the first report.

## 6. Let the schedule run [#6-let-the-schedule-run]

Start the server and leave it running:

```sh
bun run dev
```

Nile Js starts the schedule when the server boots. The job runs at its next time, and the scheduler skips a run if the previous one is still active. Check the next time at any point by calling `server.scheduler.inspect()` from code, as the script does.

## 7. Type-check [#7-type-check]

```sh
./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit
```

You should see no output and exit with status 0.

## Limits in this example [#limits-in-this-example]

- The schedule runs in every process that has it enabled. Running two replicas produces two reports, so keep this server to one process, or move the schedule to a separate scheduler process.
- A missed run is not replayed after a restart.
- The queue lives in memory. A report waiting in the queue is lost if the process stops before it writes the file.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

- **`Port 8000 is in use` or `EADDRINUSE`.** Stop `bun run dev` before you run the script.
- **`Scheduler is not running`.** The script could not find the scheduler. Check that `src/index.ts` passes `schedules` to `createNileServer`.
- **The file is missing from `outbox`.** Look for a `failed` event in the server output. The job returns the failure from the queue.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Cron jobs](/guide/features/cron-jobs) explains every schedule form and the recorder.
- [Queues, debounce and throttle](/guide/features/queues-debounce-throttle) explains concurrency and capacity.
- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) covers scheduler lifecycle and replicas.


---

# API discovery and schemas

Discovery answers two questions for tools and agents: which services and actions exist, and what input each action expects. It uses the same `POST /api/services` endpoint as ordinary calls, with the `explore` and `schema` intents. It is off unless you enable it.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use discovery when an integration, a code generator or an AI agent needs the current action list and their input shapes. Keep it away from browsers and public clients. Discovery describes actions; it does not authorize calling them.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This server enables discovery with a secret. The helper function runs on a trusted server and asks for one action's schema. `config.discoverySecret` comes from your configuration module.

```ts
import { createNileServer, createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok, safeTry, type Result } from "slang-ts";

export const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "projects",
    description: "Project operations",
    actions: [],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "team-workspace",
  services: services,
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
    discovery: {
      enabled: true,
      secret: config.discoverySecret,
      cacheSchemas: true,
    },
  },
});

type DiscoveryDocument = {
  status: boolean;
  message: string;
  data: Record<string, unknown>;
};

/** Runs on a trusted integration server, never in a browser bundle. */
export const fetchActionSchema = async (
  service: string,
  action: string
): Promise<Result<DiscoveryDocument, string>> => {
  const response = await safeTry(() =>
    fetch("https://api.example.com/api/services", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        intent: "schema",
        service: service,
        action: action,
        payload: { discoverySecret: config.discoverySecret },
      }),
    })
  );

  if (response.isErr) {
    return Err("Discovery request failed");
  }

  const document = (await response.value.json()) as DiscoveryDocument;
  if (!document.status) {
    return Err(document.message);
  }

  return Ok(document);
};
```

Requests to `explore` and `schema` must include `discoverySecret` in the payload. A header or a JWT does not satisfy the gate.

Without the secret, the server refuses the request:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Invalid or missing discovery secret",
  "data": {}
}
```

With the secret, `explore` lists services and their action names. A `schema` request for one action returns its JSON Schema under the action name. An action without validation returns `null`:

```json
{
  "status": true,
  "message": "Schema for 'account.ping'",
  "data": { "ping": null }
}
```

## Intents and wildcards [#intents-and-wildcards]

| Intent | Service | Action | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `"*"` | `"*"` | Every service with its action names. |
| `explore` | `"name"` | `"*"` | Action summaries for one service. |
| `explore` | `"name"` | `"name"` | Details for one action. |
| `schema` | `"name"` | `"name"` | JSON Schema for one action, keyed by the action name. |
| `schema` | `"*"` or `"name"` | `"*"` | Schemas for several actions. |

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `rest.discovery.enabled` | Turns discovery on. Off by default. |
| `rest.discovery.secret` | Value that must appear as `payload.discoverySecret`. If it is unset, the gate does not check a secret, so set one. |
| `rest.discovery.cacheSchemas` | Caches JSON Schema conversions. On by default. |
| Action `cacheSchema` | Set `false` to convert that action's schema on every request. |
| Action `visibility.rest` | Set `false` to leave the action out of detailed schema output. |

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- Schemas are converted only when a schema request needs them. Ordinary calls never convert them.
- The JSON Schema describes the Zod input. Refinements, transforms and defaults may become looser descriptions, so the server still validates every call.
- Replacing an action's `validation` schema object refreshes its cached conversion. Changing fields on the same object can leave the cache stale.
- Discovery does not run JWT checks or role hooks. Anyone with the secret can read the descriptions.

## Limits [#limits]

- The stock `@nilejs/client` `explore` and `schema` methods send an empty payload, so they cannot pass the secret. Use a plain `fetch` on a trusted server, as in the example.
- Discovery is not a permission system. Keep the secret out of browser bundles and public repositories.
- `visibility.rest: false` hides an action's detail, but the service list can still show its name.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Enabling discovery without a secret in production. Without a secret, the gate does not check anything.
- Putting the discovery secret in a frontend bundle.
- Assuming schema output is filtered to the caller's role.
- Treating a tool description as permission to call an action. Call actions through your normal authentication.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Discovery and agents](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents) explains how to connect a tool to discovery.
- [Build with AI agents](/guide/agents) describes the agent workflow and the Nile Js skill.
- [Authentication and hooks](/guide/features/authentication-and-hooks) covers the checks that still apply to a call.


---

# Authentication and hooks

Nile Js verifies JWTs for actions you mark as protected, and it runs hooks around every action. Use the built-in verifier for identity, a global before hook for policy such as roles, and local hooks for steps that belong to one action.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use `isProtected` for any action that needs a signed-in user. Use `accessControl` to list the roles an action requires, then enforce that list in a hook, because Nile stores the labels but does not check them. Use local hooks when one action needs a shared step, such as loading a policy, before its handler runs.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This file configures JWT verification and a global before hook that checks every role an action lists. `config.jwtSecret` comes from your configuration module and must stay on the server.

```ts
import {
  type BeforeActionHandler,
  createAction,
  createNileServer,
  createServices,
} from "@nilejs/nile";
import type { NileContext } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok, type Result } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";

const requireRolesHook: BeforeActionHandler<boolean, string> = ({
  nileContext,
  action,
}): Result<boolean, string> => {
  if (!action.isProtected) {
    return Ok(true);
  }

  const session = nileContext.getSession("rest");
  if (session === undefined) {
    return Err("Sign in to continue");
  }

  const requiredRoles = action.accessControl ?? [];
  if (requiredRoles.length === 0) {
    return Ok(true);
  }

  const roles = session.roles;
  const hasEveryRole =
    Array.isArray(roles) &&
    requiredRoles.every((role) => roles.includes(role));

  if (!hasEveryRole) {
    return Err("Access denied");
  }

  return Ok(true);
};

const profileSchema = z.object({
  includeOrganization: z.boolean().optional().default(false),
});

type ProfileInput = z.infer<typeof profileSchema>;

const profileHandler = (
  input: ProfileInput,
  context?: NileContext<unknown>
) => {
  const session = context?.getSession("rest");
  if (session === undefined) {
    return Err("Sign in to continue");
  }

  return Ok({
    userId: session.userId,
    organizationId: input.includeOrganization ? session.organizationId : null,
  });
};

const profileAction = createAction<ProfileInput>({
  name: "profile",
  description: "Read the signed-in user profile",
  isProtected: true,
  validation: profileSchema,
  handler: profileHandler,
});

const invoicesAction = createAction<ProfileInput>({
  name: "invoices",
  description: "List invoices for billing administrators",
  isProtected: true,
  accessControl: ["billing-admin"],
  validation: profileSchema,
  handler: profileHandler,
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "account",
    description: "Account operations",
    actions: [profileAction, invoicesAction],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "team-workspace",
  services: services,
  auth: { secret: config.jwtSecret, method: "header" },
  onBeforeActionHandler: requireRolesHook,
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"] },
});
```

The `account.profile` action needs any valid token. The `account.invoices` action needs a token whose `roles` claim includes `billing-admin`. The runnable version of this pattern, with token generation and requests, is in [the protected profile example](/guide/examples/protected-profile).

With no token, a protected action returns:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "No JWT token found in header",
  "data": {}
}
```

A token that is valid but lacks the required role returns `Access denied` with the same envelope. Both are HTTP 400.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Where | Option | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server | `auth.secret` | Key used to verify tokens. Required when any action is protected. |
| Server | `auth.method` | `"header"` (default) reads `Authorization: Bearer`. `"cookie"` reads `auth_token` by default. |
| Server | `auth.headerName`, `auth.cookieName`, `auth.algorithm` | Change the source header or cookie name, or the algorithm (`HS256` by default). |
| Server | `onBeforeActionHandler` | Global check that runs for every action, after JWT verification. |
| Action | `isProtected` | Requires verified JWT. Both `auth` and `isProtected` must be set. |
| Action | `accessControl` | Role labels. Enforced only by your hook. |
| Action | `hooks.before`, `hooks.after` | Local hooks that run another action's handler. Set `isCritical` to decide whether a failure stops the action. |

The verifier requires `userId` (or `id` or `sub`) and `organizationId` (or `organization_id` or `orgId`) as non-empty strings. Other claims, such as `roles`, remain on the request session as `getSession("rest")`.

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- Nile runs JWT verification first for protected actions, then the global before hook, then local before hooks, validation, the handler, local after hooks and the global after hook.
- The global before hook runs for every action. Return `Ok(true)` to continue. Its returned value does not replace the payload.
- A local hook runs its referenced action's handler directly. It does not run that action's JWT check, validation or hooks. Put required checks inside the hook's handler.
- Unprotected actions skip token verification. Sending a token to them does not populate their session.
- `auth` also verifies tokens from HTTP requests for protected actions. Custom routes do not run the action check. Use `verifyJWT` there, as shown in [authentication](/guide/basics/auth).

## Limits [#limits]

- Verification failures return a fixed message: `JWT authentication failed: token expired`, `JWT authentication failed: invalid token`, or a short reason for issuer, audience, algorithm or timing problems. The message never contains the token, its header or its claims, so it is safe to log.
- Role checks only protect the actions that use them. Check resource ownership inside the domain operation.
- Discovery has its own secret gate. It does not inherit JWT or role checks.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Setting `isProtected` without an `auth` block. Protection needs both.
- Writing `accessControl` and expecting Nile to enforce it. Your hook must read `action.accessControl`.
- Trusting an `organizationId` in the payload. Compare it with the verified session.
- Putting the JWT secret in client code or in a committed file.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Authentication](/guide/basics/auth) covers the session fields and external providers.
- [Hooks and pipelines](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines) gives the full order of steps.
- [Composing hooks](/guide/advanced/composing-hooks) shows a multi-step local hook pipeline.
- [Protected profile example](/guide/examples/protected-profile) runs this pattern end to end.


---

# HTTP, WebSocket and direct calls

Every action runs through the same pipeline no matter how it was called: validation, hooks, the handler and the JWT check for protected actions. The transport changes how you send the request and how the response arrives. This page shows the three paths and what each one needs.

## When to use each path [#when-to-use-each-path]

| Path | Use it for | Requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP `POST /api/services` | Browsers, mobile apps, curl and any HTTP client | `intent`, `service`, `action` and `payload` in the body |
| Socket client `invoke` | Clients that already hold a socket connection for topics | An authenticated socket connection |
| `server.invoke` | Jobs, scheduled work and other code in the same backend | Credentials for protected actions |

## HTTP [#http]

Every operation is a `POST` to the services endpoint. The `intent` field selects `execute`, `explore` or `schema`:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"intent":"execute","service":"tasks","action":"list","payload":{}}'
```

A successful call returns `status: true` with the handler's object as `data`:

```json
{
  "status": true,
  "message": "Action 'tasks.list' executed",
  "data": {
    "tasks": []
  }
}
```

A failed call returns `status: false` and HTTP 400. Read the `status` field as well as the HTTP status.

## Socket client [#socket-client]

The dedicated socket client sends `invoke` over the same connection that receives topic messages. Use the same payload types as the HTTP client:

```ts
const changed = await socket.invoke({
  service: "orders",
  action: "set-status",
  payload: { orderId: orderId, status: "packed" },
});

if (changed.isErr) {
  console.error(changed.error, changed.details);
  return;
}

console.log(changed.value);
```

Protected actions use the identity that the server verified when the socket connected. See [sockets and typed messages](/guide/reference/realtime) for the connection setup.

## Direct calls with `server.invoke` [#direct-calls-with-serverinvoke]

`server.invoke` runs an action in the same process without a network request. It is the right call from a scheduled job or from backend code that already has a server instance:

```ts
const result = await server.invoke({
  service: "orders",
  action: "create",
  payload: { customerId: customerId, total: 0 },
  requestId: "job-create-order-1",
});

if (result.isErr) {
  return Err(result.error);
}

return Ok(result.value);
```

The optional fields are:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `requestId` | Correlates logs and telemetry for this call. |
| `signal` | Cancels the call. Nested calls inherit it. |
| `credentials` | Headers to verify for a protected action. Required when the action is protected. |
| `session` | Trusted application session for the call. It does not skip JWT verification. |
| `clientKey` | Identity used for rate limits. |

Calling a protected action without `credentials` returns `Err("Authentication required: no request context available")`. Pass the verified headers, as the socket transport does, or call an unprotected action instead.

An action with `visibility: { rpc: false }` cannot be called through `server.invoke`. Set `rpc.enabled: false` on the server to turn the direct interface off entirely.

## Limits [#limits]

- Timeouts apply to HTTP and direct calls through `execution.timeoutMs`. A timed-out call stops waiting, but code that ignores its signal keeps running.
- Writes made before a timeout or a failure are not rolled back.
- The socket client has a finite acknowledgement timeout. A timeout does not prove that the write did not commit.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Sending a multipart upload to a JSON action, or a JSON body to an upload action. See [file uploads](/guide/features/file-uploads).
- Calling `server.invoke` for a protected action without credentials.
- Passing a client-supplied `session` into `server.invoke` and expecting it to replace JWT verification.
- Reading `value` before checking `isErr` on the client.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) explains direct calls, cancellation and correlation IDs.
- [Sockets and typed messages](/guide/reference/realtime) describes the socket contract.
- [Testing actions](/guide/advanced/testing-actions) uses `server.invoke` in tests.


---

# Context and logging

A handler receives the execution's `NileContext` as its second argument. Use it for shared resources such as the logger and database, the signed-in session, and the request identifier for correlating logs. Use the logger for records you choose to write.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Read `context.resources` when a handler needs the logger or database. Read `getSession("rest")` for the signed-in user. Read `context.execution` for the request ID, transport and cancellation signal. Use `updateHookState` for state that belongs to one execution. Use `set` and `get` only for application-wide values.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

The server registers a logger and a database as resources. The handler writes one log entry per outcome and includes the request's identifiers in the data it logs.

```ts
import {
  createAction,
  createLogger,
  createNileServer,
  createServices,
  type NileContext,
} from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";

const logger = createLogger("team-workspace", {
  mode: "prod",
  chunking: "daily",
});

const renameProjectSchema = z.object({
  projectId: z.string().uuid(),
  name: z.string().trim().min(1, "Name is required"),
});

type RenameProjectInput = z.infer<typeof renameProjectSchema>;

const renameProjectHandler = (
  input: RenameProjectInput,
  context?: NileContext<unknown>
) => {
  const activeLogger = context?.resources?.logger;

  if (input.name === "system") {
    activeLogger?.warn({
      atFunction: "renameProject",
      message: "Rejected a reserved project name",
      data: { projectId: input.projectId },
    });
    return Err("Choose a different project name");
  }

  activeLogger?.info({
    atFunction: "renameProject",
    message: "Project renamed",
    data: { projectId: input.projectId },
  });

  return Ok({ projectId: input.projectId, name: input.name });
};

const renameProjectAction = createAction<RenameProjectInput>({
  name: "rename",
  description: "Rename a project",
  validation: renameProjectSchema,
  handler: renameProjectHandler,
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "projects",
    description: "Project operations",
    actions: [renameProjectAction],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "team-workspace",
  services: services,
  resources: { logger: logger },
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"] },
});
```

Handlers are typed with `NileContext<unknown>` and read optional fields with `?.`. Nile passes the context on every call, including `server.invoke` calls. The fields are optional because your handler can also be called from a test or a background job that has no request.

With the logger above, `createLogger` writes structured lines to `logs/` relative to the working directory. The starter's startup line looks like this:

```text
22:31:21.321 INFO  onBoot my-app booted - PGLite schema ready
```

## What the context gives you [#what-the-context-gives-you]

| Location | Scope | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `context.resources` | Shared across requests, set at server creation | Logger, database and other application resources |
| `context.getSession("rest")` | One request | Verified identity from `auth`, such as `userId` and `organizationId` |
| `context.execution` | One execution | `requestId`, `transport`, `signal`, `clientKey`, optional `traceId` |
| `context.updateHookState(key, value)` and `context.hookContext.state` | One action execution | Values passed between hooks and the handler |
| `context.set(key, value)` and `context.get(key)` | Shared by every request | Application-wide values, such as a feature flag |

Use `getContext<AppDatabase>()` outside a handler when you need the typed resources, for example in a module that does not receive the context. It throws if the server has not been created.

## Logger options [#logger-options]

| Option | Values | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `"prod"`, `"dev"`, `"agentic"` | Output format. `dev` is readable in a terminal, `prod` is structured for collection. |
| `chunking` | `"none"`, `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, `"monthly"` | How files are split under `logs/`. Nile does not delete old files. |

Each entry includes the application name, the function name you pass as `atFunction`, the message, your optional `data` and a log ID. Nile attaches execution IDs to related log entries.

## Limits [#limits]

- `context.set` writes to a map in this process. Other instances do not see it, and a restart clears it.
- A logger resource does not record every request. Log the events you need.
- Time-based chunking does not ship or delete logs. Plan retention for your deployment.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Storing the current user with `set("user", ...)`. Concurrent requests share that value. Read the session instead.
- Logging passwords, tokens or personal data in `data`. Log identifiers and outcomes.
- Calling `getContext` at module load before `createNileServer` has run.
- Assuming `context.execution` exists outside an execution. Read it with `?.`.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Context](/guide/basics/context) explains shared and request-scoped state.
- [Logging](/guide/internals/logging) covers file layout and reading logs.
- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) describes execution IDs, telemetry and log filters.


---

# Cron jobs

Scheduled jobs run business functions on a timetable without an HTTP request. Each job has a name, a schedule and a handler. Nile Js starts the schedules when the server boots and reports each run to a recorder you provide.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use a schedule for work that happens on a timetable: a weekly report, a nightly cleanup or a reminder at a fixed time. Put the work in an ordinary function and let the job call it, so the same function can run from an action or a test.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

The job builds a summary and returns a Result. The recorder receives start, completion and failure events. This file registers the schedule with the server; the [weekly report example](/guide/examples/weekly-report) adds a queue and runs the job end to end.

```ts
import {
  createNileServer,
  createServices,
  type JobRunContext,
  type JobRunEvent,
  type SchedulerOptions,
} from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";

type WeeklySummary = {
  orderCount: number;
  generatedAt: string;
};

const buildWeeklySummary = async (signal: AbortSignal): Promise<WeeklySummary> => {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    throw new Error("Report was cancelled");
  }
  await Promise.resolve();
  return { orderCount: 0, generatedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
};

const weeklyReportJob = async (run: JobRunContext) => {
  const summary = await buildWeeklySummary(run.signal);
  if (summary.orderCount < 0) {
    return Err("Summary is invalid");
  }
  return Ok(summary);
};

const recordRunEvent = async (event: JobRunEvent): Promise<void> => {
  await Promise.resolve(event.job);
};

export const schedules: SchedulerOptions = {
  jobs: [
    {
      name: "weekly-report",
      schedule: {
        weekly: "monday",
        at: "09:00",
        timezone: "Africa/Kampala",
      },
      handler: weeklyReportJob,
    },
  ],
  onRunEvent: recordRunEvent,
  onRecorderError: (job: string) => {
    console.error(`Could not record run event for ${job}`);
  },
};

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "reports",
    description: "Scheduled reports",
    actions: [],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "back-office",
  services: services,
  schedules: schedules,
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://ops.example.com"] },
});
```

`buildWeeklySummary` is your application function. Replace it with a real query. Nile passes a `JobRunContext` with the job name, run ID, scheduled time and an abort signal. Pass that signal to any work that can be cancelled.

Running the same job by hand is useful in tests and runbooks. `server.scheduler.runNow("weekly-report")` runs it now and returns its Result. In the example project this printed:

```text
jobs: [{"name":"weekly-report","running":true,"active":false,"nextRun":"2026-10-26T06:00:00.000Z"}]
runNow: {"report":"weekly-2026-10-22","path":"outbox/weekly-2026-10-22.json"}
```

## Schedule forms [#schedule-forms]

| Schedule | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Midnight | `{ midnight: true, timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }` | Every midnight in the timezone. |
| Daily | `{ daily: true, at: "09:00", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }` | Once a day at the time given. |
| Weekly | `{ weekly: "monday", at: "09:00", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }` | Once a week on the named day. `at` is optional. |
| Cron | `{ cron: "0 9 * * 1-5", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }` | Standard five-field cron expression. |
| One time | `{ once: "2027-01-01T09:00:00+03:00" }` | Requires an offset and a future date at registration. |
| Interval | `{ every: "15m" }` or a number of milliseconds | Waits for the previous run to finish, then waits the interval. |

Calendar schedules use UTC when you omit `timezone`.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `jobs[].name` | Unique job name, used by `runNow` and `inspect`. |
| `jobs[].handler` | Function that receives `JobRunContext`. It may return a value or a Result. |
| `onRunEvent` | Receives `started`, `completed`, `failed` and `skipped` events. |
| `onRecorderError` | Called when recording an event fails. Business work continues. |
| `recorderTimeoutMs`, `recorderCapacity` | Bounds for the recorder. |

`server.scheduler` exposes `inspect()`, `runNow(name)`, `start()`, `stop()` and `drain()`.

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- Overlapping runs are skipped. A job that is still running when its next time arrives does not start a second copy.
- Missed runs are not replayed after a restart.
- Interval jobs wait for the previous run to finish before counting the interval.
- Failures and return values are not stored automatically. Your recorder decides what to keep.
- A stopped scheduler does not restart. Create a new server instance to schedule again.

## Limits [#limits]

- Every process that has schedules enabled runs them. Two replicas run each job twice unless you run schedules in one process or use an external scheduler.
- One-time jobs are not stored, so a restart before their time forgets them.
- Recording events does not make a run durable.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Enabling schedules on every replica of a web service and assuming each job runs once.
- Forgetting `timezone`. Calendar jobs then run at UTC times.
- Writing the business logic inside the job object. Keep it in a function you can test and call from an action.
- Ignoring the `Err` from a job. Return a Result and record the failure.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) covers the scheduler lifecycle and the recorder.
- [Queues, debounce and throttle](/guide/features/queues-debounce-throttle) limits how a job's work runs.
- [Weekly report example](/guide/examples/weekly-report) runs a scheduled job end to end.


---

# Database models

`createModel` turns a Drizzle table into a set of helpers that return Results. Your actions call the helpers instead of building queries inline, and validation, error handling and pagination follow one pattern across the application.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use a model for each table that actions read or write. Keep joins, reports and custom queries next to the model in the same domain folder, and use the table and schemas the model exposes when you write them.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

The table is an ordinary Drizzle table. The model is created from it with a database client. The action validates input with Zod, calls `create`, and returns the saved row or the failure.

```ts
import { createAction, createModel, createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { pgTable, text, timestamp, uuid } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";
import { z } from "zod";

export const tasks = pgTable("tasks", {
  id: uuid("id").defaultRandom().primaryKey(),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
  description: text("description"),
  status: text("status", { enum: ["pending", "in-progress", "done"] })
    .notNull()
    .default("pending"),
  created_at: timestamp("created_at", { withTimezone: true })
    .notNull()
    .defaultNow(),
  updated_at: timestamp("updated_at", { withTimezone: true })
    .notNull()
    .defaultNow(),
});

export const taskModel = createModel(tasks, {
  db: database,
  name: "task",
});

const createTaskSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1, "Title is required"),
  description: z.string().optional().default(""),
});

type CreateTaskInput = z.infer<typeof createTaskSchema>;

const createTaskHandler = async (input: CreateTaskInput) => {
  const created = await taskModel.create({
    data: {
      title: input.title,
      description: input.description,
    },
  });

  if (created.isErr) {
    return Err(created.error);
  }

  return Ok({ task: created.value });
};

const createTaskAction = createAction<CreateTaskInput>({
  name: "create",
  description: "Create a task",
  validation: createTaskSchema,
  handler: createTaskHandler,
});

const listTasksHandler = async () => {
  const page = await taskModel.findPaginated({ limit: 20, offset: 0 });

  if (page.isErr) {
    return Err(page.error);
  }

  return Ok({ tasks: page.value.items, hasMore: page.value.hasMore });
};

const listTasksAction = createAction<undefined>({
  name: "list",
  description: "List the first page of tasks",
  handler: listTasksHandler,
});

export const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "tasks",
    description: "Task management",
    actions: [createTaskAction, listTasksAction],
  },
]);
```

The `database` value is the Drizzle client your application creates. It is declared as a global in the snippet so the file type-checks on its own. The starter's `src/db/client.ts` creates it for you.

## Methods [#methods]

| Method | Success value | Failure when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `create({ data, dbx? })` | Inserted row | Data does not match the insert schema, or the insert fails. |
| `findById(id)` | Matching row | No row matches. |
| `update({ id, data, dbx? })` | Updated row | No row matches, or data does not match the update schema. |
| `delete(id)` | Deleted row | No row matches. |
| `findAll()` | Array of rows | The query fails. An empty table returns an empty array. |
| `findPaginated({ limit?, offset? })` | `{ items, total, hasMore }` | The query fails. |
| `findPaginated({ limit?, cursor, cursorColumn? })` | `{ items, nextCursor, hasMore }` | The query fails. |

Each method returns a Result. Check `isErr` before reading `value`.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Readable label used in error messages and logs. |
| `db` | Drizzle client. If omitted, the model reads `resources.database` from the current context when a method runs. |
| `cursorColumn` | Column used for cursor pages. Defaults to `id`. |
| `limit` | Page size for `findPaginated`. Defaults to 50. |

The model also exposes `table` and `schemas.insert`, `schemas.update` and `schemas.select`. Use them in custom queries so they stay in step with the table.

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- `create` and `update` check the data against the generated Zod schemas before they query. They write the data you supplied.
- Offset pagination uses a count of the whole table. Cursor pages fetch one extra row to decide whether another page exists.
- `findAll` and offset pagination sort by `created_at` when the table has it. Otherwise no default order applies.
- Query failures are logged with bounded diagnostics and returned as a safe failure. Driver messages that may contain data are not returned.
- `createTx` and `updateTx` run inside a transaction only when you pass `dbx`. Omitting `dbx` does not start one.

## Limits [#limits]

- The helpers cover single-table work. Multi-step writes need an explicit transaction.
- Cursor pages need a column that is unique and ordered. `id` works for UUIDs only if it sorts the way you want.
- A transaction-wrapped Err is thrown to roll back. Guard that call with `safeTry`.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Treating a missing row as `null`. `findById` returns a failure, so check `isErr`.
- Calling `createTx` without `dbx`, then expecting rollback on failure.
- Paginating with a non-unique cursor column. Rows with the same value can be skipped or repeated.
- Writing raw SQL in the action when a model method covers the case.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Model helpers](/guide/internals/db/create-model) has the complete method reference.
- [Data access overview](/guide/internals/db/) covers multi-write workflows.
- [Shared utilities](/guide/reference/shared-utilities) explains `dbTry` and safe database failures.


---

# File uploads

An upload is an action whose input arrives as multipart form data. Nile Js parses the form, applies the limits in `rest.uploads`, and passes the fields and files to your handler as a structured payload. Nile Js does not store the files; your handler decides where they go.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use an upload action when a client sends a document or image with other fields in one request. Set `isSpecial: { contentType: "multipart/form-data" }` on the action so Nile Js routes the request to the form parser and rejects JSON bodies for it.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

The server sets the limits. The action reads one `document` file and one `title` field. The handler returns the file's name, type and size; a real action would save the file to storage.

```ts
import {
  createAction,
  createNileServer,
  createServices,
  type StructuredPayload,
} from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";

const inspectDocumentHandler = (payload: StructuredPayload) => {
  const document = payload.files.document;
  const title = payload.fields.title;

  if (!(document instanceof File)) {
    return Err("Send one document");
  }

  if (typeof title !== "string") {
    return Err("A title is required");
  }

  return Ok({
    title: title,
    filename: document.name,
    size: document.size,
  });
};

const inspectDocumentAction = createAction<StructuredPayload>({
  name: "inspect",
  description: "Inspect an uploaded PDF or image",
  isSpecial: { contentType: "multipart/form-data" },
  handler: inspectDocumentHandler,
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "documents",
    description: "Document intake",
    actions: [inspectDocumentAction],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "documents",
  services: services,
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
    uploads: {
      enforceContentType: true,
      limits: {
        maxFiles: 3,
        maxFileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
        maxTotalSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
        minFileSize: 1,
        maxFilenameLength: 128,
      },
      allow: {
        mimeTypes: ["image/png", "image/jpeg", "application/pdf"],
        extensions: [".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".pdf"],
      },
    },
  },
});

export const uploadDocument = async (): Promise<void> => {
  const formData = new FormData();
  formData.append("intent", "execute");
  formData.append("service", "documents");
  formData.append("action", "inspect");
  formData.append("title", "Project brief");
  formData.append("document", selectedFile);

  const response = await fetch("https://app.example.com/api/services", {
    method: "POST",
    body: formData,
  });
  console.log(response.status);
};
```

The client sends the same request with the `upload` method of `@nilejs/client`:

```ts
import { createNileClient } from "@nilejs/client";

interface DocumentPayloads {
  documents: {
    inspect: { title: string };
  };
}

const nile = createNileClient<DocumentPayloads>({
  baseUrl: "https://app.example.com/api",
});

export const uploadBrief = async (): Promise<void> => {
  const result = await nile.upload({
    service: "documents",
    action: "inspect",
    files: { document: selectedFile },
    fields: { title: "Project brief" },
  });

  if (result.isErr) {
    console.error(result.error, result.details);
    return;
  }

  console.log(result.value);
};
```

The request can also be sent with curl. The routing fields `intent`, `service` and `action` go in the form with the other fields:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -F 'intent=execute' -F 'service=documents' -F 'action=inspect' \
  -F 'title=Project brief' -F 'document=@./brief.pdf;type=application/pdf'
```

With a 9-byte PDF named `tiny.pdf`, the example project returned:

```json
{
  "status": true,
  "message": "Action 'documents.inspect' executed",
  "data": {
    "title": "Project brief",
    "filename": "tiny.pdf",
    "contentType": "application/pdf",
    "size": 9
  }
}
```

The complete runnable project, including oversized and wrong-type checks, is in [the file upload example](/guide/examples/file-upload).

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `rest.uploads.limits.maxFiles` | Most files in one request. |
| `rest.uploads.limits.maxFileSize`, `minFileSize` | Largest and smallest size for one file. A zero-byte file is rejected by default. |
| `rest.uploads.limits.maxTotalSize` | Combined size of all files. |
| `rest.uploads.limits.maxFilenameLength` | Longest file name accepted. |
| `rest.uploads.allow.mimeTypes`, `allow.extensions` | Types and extensions a file must match. |
| `rest.uploads.enforceContentType` | Checks the request type against the action's `isSpecial.contentType`. |
| `rest.protection.maxBodyBytes` | Largest request body read before parsing. Default 10 MiB. |

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- The handler receives `{ fields, files }`. A repeated key becomes an array.
- Using the same key for a file and a text field is rejected, whatever `uploadMode` is set to.
- Each file is checked in this order: name length, zero bytes, minimum size, file count, maximum size, total size, then the type and extension allowlist.
- A JSON request to a multipart action returns HTTP 400. The response names what the action expects:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Action 'documents.inspect' expects multipart/form-data. Send the request as form data with its files.",
  "data": {
    "error_category": "validation",
    "expected": "multipart/form-data",
    "received": "application/json"
  }
}
```

- A multipart request to an action that declares a different `isSpecial.contentType`, such as `application/json`, returns HTTP 415 with `data.expected` and `data.received`.
- A file over the limit returns a failure with `error_category: "validation"`, the limit name, the maximum and the offending files. In the example project, a 6 MiB file returned `upload limit exceeded` with `"limit":"maxFileSize","max":5242880`.
- A multipart request to an ordinary action that does not declare `isSpecial` runs as that action. Use this only for actions that do not need files.

## Limits [#limits]

- Validation trusts the declared type and the file extension. It does not inspect the file's bytes. In the example, a text file named `fake.png` with type `image/png` was accepted. Check the content in your handler when it matters.
- The whole body is read before parsing. A request larger than `maxBodyBytes` is refused even when each file is within its own limit. Raise `maxBodyBytes` when `maxTotalSize` is larger than the default 10 MiB, plus room for the form fields.
- Nile Js does not scan for malware, store files or enforce who may download them. Those belong to your application.
- Buffered parsing holds the upload in memory while it is handled.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Trusting `file.type` for security. Check the bytes, or store the file and process it in an isolated worker.
- Setting `maxTotalSize` above `maxBodyBytes` and wondering why large uploads fail.
- Sending JSON to an upload action, or a multipart body to a JSON action.
- Forgetting authentication. Mark the upload action `isProtected` and configure `auth` when files are private.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Uploads](/guide/basics/uploads) has the full configuration reference.
- [File serving](/guide/basics/file-serving) covers returning files to clients.
- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) describes request body limits and client addresses.


---

# Features

Each page below covers one capability of Nile Js: what it does, when to use it, a complete example, the options that matter and the limits to plan for. Start with the page that matches your task. Pages link to the deeper reference when you need every option.

| Feature | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| [Validation and errors](/guide/features/validation-and-errors) | Reject bad input with Zod and return expected failures as Results |
| [Authentication and hooks](/guide/features/authentication-and-hooks) | Protect actions with JWT, enforce roles and run checks before or after an action |
| [Context and logging](/guide/features/context-and-logging) | Read shared resources, the current session and execution details, and write structured logs |
| [Queues, debounce and throttle](/guide/features/queues-debounce-throttle) | Limit concurrency, collapse repeated calls and cap how often work runs |
| [Telemetry](/guide/features/telemetry) | Send traces and metrics for actions to an OpenTelemetry collector |
| [WebSockets](/guide/features/websockets) | Publish typed topic messages to subscribers that pass your access policy |
| [Cron jobs](/guide/features/cron-jobs) | Run recurring business work on calendar, interval or one-time schedules |
| [Database models](/guide/features/database-models) | Create, read, update and delete rows through typed model helpers |
| [API discovery and schemas](/guide/features/api-discovery) | Let trusted tools list services and read action input schemas |
| [HTTP, WebSocket and direct calls](/guide/features/calling-actions) | Call the same action from HTTP, a socket client or your own backend code |
| [Retries and utilities](/guide/features/retries-and-utilities) | Retry external calls with jitter, store values briefly and wrap database failures |
| [Rate limiting](/guide/features/rate-limiting) | Bound how often a client can call an action or an HTTP route |
| [File uploads](/guide/features/file-uploads) | Accept multipart files with size, count and type limits |
| [Readiness and shutdown](/guide/features/readiness-and-shutdown) | Report readiness to a platform and stop new work before the process exits |

Ready to build something end to end? The [examples](/guide/examples) combine several of these features in complete projects.
