# Queues, debounce and throttle

Nile Js provides function controls for work that should not run in parallel, repeat too often or pile up. Each control wraps one task function and returns a `run` method that resolves with a Result. The controls live in memory, so they apply to one process.

## When to use each control [#when-to-use-each-control]

| Control | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `createQueue` | Work must run one or a few at a time, such as sending email. Callers wait in line. |
| `createDebounce` | Only the latest input matters, such as saving a draft after typing stops. Replaced callers fail. |
| `createThrottle` | The task may run at most once per window, such as refreshing a cache. |
| `createBatch` | Items should be grouped and processed together. Each item gets its own Result. |

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This module defines a receipt queue with two workers, a draft debounce and a cache throttle. Create each control once at module level so every request shares it.

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { type Result, Ok } from "slang-ts";

type ReceiptEmail = {
  orderId: string;
  to: string;
};

type SendReceiptResult = {
  sent: boolean;
};

const deliverEmail = async (
  message: ReceiptEmail,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<void> => {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    return;
  }
  await Promise.resolve(message);
};

const sendReceiptTask = async (
  email: ReceiptEmail,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<Result<SendReceiptResult, string>> => {
  await deliverEmail(email, signal);
  return Ok({ sent: true });
};

/** At most two receipts are sent at once; up to 200 more wait in line. */
export const receiptQueue = utils.createQueue<ReceiptEmail, SendReceiptResult>({
  task: sendReceiptTask,
  concurrency: 2,
  capacity: 200,
});

type DraftSave = {
  documentId: string;
  body: string;
};

const saveDraftTask = async (draft: DraftSave): Promise<{ savedAt: string }> => {
  await Promise.resolve(draft.documentId);
  return { savedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
};

/** Saves only the latest draft after the editor has been quiet for 500 ms. */
export const draftDebounce = utils.createDebounce<DraftSave, { savedAt: string }>({
  task: saveDraftTask,
  waitMs: 500,
});

type CacheRefresh = {
  region: string;
};

const refreshCacheTask = async (refresh: CacheRefresh): Promise<void> => {
  await Promise.resolve(refresh.region);
};

/** Runs the first refresh immediately, then at most once per second. */
export const cacheRefreshThrottle = utils.createThrottle<CacheRefresh, void>({
  task: refreshCacheTask,
  waitMs: 1000,
  leading: true,
  trailing: false,
});
```

Call a control from an action handler and read the Result:

```ts
const sent = await receiptQueue.run(
  { orderId: order.id, to: buyer.email },
  { signal: context?.execution?.signal }
);

if (sent.isErr) {
  return Err(sent.error);
}
```

`run` also accepts `{ signal }` so a cancelled request stops waiting. Queued work that has already started keeps its concurrency slot until it finishes.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Factory | Options | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createQueue` | `task`, `concurrency`, `capacity` | `concurrency` 1, `capacity` 1000 pending calls |
| `createDebounce` | `task`, `waitMs` | Required |
| `createThrottle` | `task`, `waitMs`, `leading`, `trailing` | `leading` true, `trailing` false |
| `createBatch` | `task`, `size`, `waitMs`, `concurrency`, `capacity` | `concurrency` 1, `capacity` 1000 buffered items |

Every control also exposes `stop()`, `drain()` and `close()`. Register it with the server so shutdown stops admission and waits for accepted work:

```ts
server.lifecycle.register(utils.createControlResource("receipt-queue", receiptQueue));
```

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- A full queue returns a failure from `run`. It does not block the caller or drop work silently.
- A debounce replaces earlier pending calls. Their `run` promises resolve with a failure, and only the last input runs.
- A throttle with `leading: true` runs the first call immediately and ignores calls in the window unless `trailing` is true.
- Tasks may return a plain value or a Result. The control unwraps the value for callers.
- Controls hold their state in memory. A restart discards pending work.

## Limits [#limits]

- Limits apply per process. Two replicas each run their own queue.
- A queue does not retry failed tasks. Use [retries](/guide/features/retries-and-utilities) inside the task when a retry is safe.
- Create controls at module level. A control created inside a handler is new for each request, so it limits nothing.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Using debounce for work where every call must run, such as recording a payment.
- Ignoring the Result of `run`.
- Forgetting to register the control, so shutdown does not wait for queued work.
- Setting `capacity` without deciding what the caller should do when the queue is full.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Shared utilities](/guide/reference/shared-utilities) covers grouped controls, idle cleanup and the retry helper.
- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) explains the control lifecycle and shutdown.
- [Weekly report example](/guide/examples/weekly-report) uses a queue inside a scheduled job.


---

# Rate limiting

Rate limiting caps how often one client can call an action. Nile Js applies the limit before the handler runs, so a client that sends a burst gets a failure instead of extra work. Limits live in memory, so each process enforces its own.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use a limit on public actions that cost money or resources, such as quotes, searches or report exports. Keep authorization for who may call an action; use rate limits for how often.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This server allows a burst of 20 quote requests per client and refills 5 per second. The key comes from `context.clientKey`, which Nile Js derives from the connection's address.

```ts
import { createAction, createNileServer, createServices, utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";

const quoteSchema = z.object({
  sku: z.string().min(1),
});

type QuoteInput = z.infer<typeof quoteSchema>;

const quoteHandler = (input: QuoteInput) => {
  return Ok({ sku: input.sku, price: 1200 });
};

const quoteAction = createAction<QuoteInput>({
  name: "quote",
  description: "Return the public price of a product",
  validation: quoteSchema,
  handler: quoteHandler,
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "catalog",
    description: "Public catalog",
    actions: [quoteAction],
  },
]);

/** Token bucket: a burst of 20 requests, refilled at 5 per second, per client. */
const quoteLimiter = utils.createRateLimiter({
  strategy: "token-bucket",
  capacity: 20,
  refillPerSecond: 5,
  maxKeys: 10_000,
});

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "catalog",
  services: services,
  execution: {
    rateLimit: {
      store: quoteLimiter,
      key: ({ context }) => context.clientKey ?? "anonymous",
    },
  },
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example.com"],
    enableStatus: true,
  },
});
```

In the example project, a loop of 25 quote requests returned HTTP 200 for the first 21 and HTTP 400 for the rest:

```text
200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 400 400 400 400
```

The denied response names the wait:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Rate limit exceeded; retry after 147ms",
  "data": {}
}
```

The 21 successes include the 20 tokens of the burst and one refill during the loop. Counts vary with timing.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `utils.createRateLimiter` `strategy` | `"token-bucket"` with `capacity` and `refillPerSecond`; `"fixed-window"` with `limit` and `windowMs`; or `"sliding-window"` with `limit` and `windowMs`. |
| `maxKeys` | Most keys the memory store holds. At the limit, new keys are refused. |
| `execution.rateLimit` | Policy for every action. |
| `execution.services[name].rateLimit` | Policy for one service. Overrides the global policy. |
| `execution.services[name].actions[name].rateLimit` | Policy for one action. Overrides the service policy. |
| `rateLimit: false` | Turns off an inherited policy for that service or action. |
| `key` | Function that returns the client key. It receives the execution details, including the verified identity. |

Policies resolve from the most specific to the least specific. Keys are computed after JWT verification and the global before hook, so you can key on a verified user or organization.

## HTTP-level limits [#http-level-limits]

`rest.rateLimiting` limits requests to the services endpoint by a header value. Use it only with a header that your proxy sets and overwrites. A client can set any header it likes, including `x-forwarded-for`, so a client-controlled header is not a verified identity. Keep this limit in place alongside the action policy when you need both.

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- A denied call returns a failure with the wait in the message. The handler does not run.
- Each `consume` call returns a Result with `allowed`, `remaining`, `retryAfterMs` and a reason when denied.
- Cooldowns are optional. Repeated denials can extend a capped cooldown.
- `reset(key)` restores a key's allowance. Use it from an operator tool.

## Limits [#limits]

- The default store is in memory. Two replicas each allow the full quota.
- A restart clears every counter.
- A shared store must check and consume atomically. Separate read and write calls can race. Nile Js does not supply Redis or database stores.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Keying on a client-controlled header.
- Using one limiter for every service without thinking about its cost. Give expensive actions their own policy.
- Expecting a limit to stop a determined attacker. Pair it with authentication and a proxy or firewall.
- Forgetting that `rateLimit: false` turns off inheritance for that service or action.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) describes the shared quota design and client addresses.
- [Shared utilities](/guide/reference/shared-utilities) covers client address normalization.
- [Public rate-limited quote example](/guide/examples/rate-limited-quote) runs this pattern end to end.


---

# Readiness and shutdown

A deployment platform needs two signals from your service: whether it is ready to receive traffic, and whether it is still running. Nile Js provides both, and a shutdown call that stops new work, waits for accepted work and closes the resources you register.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Enable the status endpoints for any service behind a load balancer or orchestrator. Call `server.lifecycle.shutdown` when your platform sends a termination signal, so in-flight requests finish before the process exits.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This server enables the status endpoints, registers its HTTP listener as a lifecycle resource and shuts down on `SIGTERM`. The `onBoot` hook runs before the server reports ready.

```ts
import { createNileServer, createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Ok } from "slang-ts";

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "health",
    description: "Service health",
    actions: [],
  },
]);

const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "team-workspace",
  services: services,
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
    enableStatus: true,
  },
  onBoot: {
    maxWaitTime: 30_000,
    fn: async (context) => {
      context.set("bootedAt", new Date().toISOString());
      return Ok(null);
    },
  },
});

const native = server.nativeRest;
if (native === undefined) {
  throw new Error("Bun native transport was not initialized");
}

const listener = Bun.serve({
  port: 8000,
  fetch: native.fetch,
});

server.lifecycle.register({
  name: "http-listener",
  stop: () => {
    listener.stop(false);
  },
  close: () => {
    listener.stop(true);
  },
});

const shutdownOnSignal = async (): Promise<void> => {
  const report = await server.lifecycle.shutdown({ timeoutMs: 10_000 });
  if (report.timedOut) {
    console.error("Shutdown timed out", report.remainingExecutions);
  }
  process.exit(0);
};

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  void shutdownOnSignal();
});
```

## Endpoints [#endpoints]

With `rest.enableStatus: true`, two `GET` endpoints appear outside `/api`:

| Endpoint | Use it for | Response while running | Response during shutdown |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/status` | Liveness: the process answers | `{"status":true,"message":"my-app is running","data":{}}` | Not part of the readiness contract |
| `/ready` | Readiness: the server accepts work | `{"status":true,"message":"Ready","data":{}}` with HTTP 200 | `{"status":false,"message":"Nile is shutting down","data":{}}` with HTTP 503 |

Point liveness probes at `/status` and readiness probes at `/ready`. Use readiness to take a replica out of rotation before it drains.

## Shutdown [#shutdown]

```ts
const report = await server.lifecycle.shutdown({ timeoutMs: 10_000 });
```

Shutdown proceeds in this order:

1. New work is refused.
2. Schedules stop admitting runs.
3. Accepted executions drain. A deadline asks them to cancel.
4. Registered resources stop, drain and close.

The report contains `timedOut`, `errors` and `remainingExecutions`. In the example server, a shutdown with nothing in flight returned:

```json
{"timedOut":false,"errors":[],"remainingExecutions":0}
```

Repeated calls share one shutdown. A deadline cannot force JavaScript to stop, so work that ignores its cancellation signal may still be running when the report returns.

## Register resources [#register-resources]

Register anything your server owns that must close in order, such as a listener, a database pool or a queue:

```ts
server.lifecycle.register({
  name: "http-listener",
  stop: () => {
    listener.stop(false);
  },
  close: () => {
    listener.stop(true);
  },
});
```

`stop` should stop accepting connections quickly. `drain` waits for work to finish, and `close` releases the resource. Register a control with `utils.createControlResource` to include a queue in the same lifecycle.

## Limits [#limits]

- Nile Js does not install signal handlers. Connect `SIGTERM` or your platform's signal to `shutdown`, as the example does.
- Shutdown does not roll back writes that were already in progress.
- Startup failures reject the boot promise after cleaning up. Your process decides whether to exit.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Exiting the process on `SIGTERM` without calling `shutdown`. In-flight requests are cut off.
- Setting a shutdown timeout longer than your platform's grace period.
- Registering a database pool without a `close` callback.
- Calling `shutdown` with a timeout longer than the grace period your platform allows.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) covers lifecycle states, cancellation and project structure.
- [Deployment](/guide/start/deploy) shows container and platform settings.
- [Getting started](/guide/start/getting-started) shows the starter's `onBoot` hook and the `/status` and `/ready` requests.


---

# Retries and utilities

Nile Js includes a few helpers for work outside the action pipeline: retries with backoff for calls to other services, a bounded in-memory store for short-lived values, and a wrapper that turns thrown database errors into safe failures. Import them from `utils` in `@nilejs/nile`.

## When to use them [#when-to-use-them]

Use `retryFnWithJitter` when you poll a provider or call a service that fails transiently and the operation is safe to repeat. Use `createMemoryStore` for values that expire quickly, such as short cache entries. Use `dbTry` around a database call that might throw.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This module polls a delivery provider with up to eight attempts and a 60-second deadline. It also keeps order summaries for 30 seconds in a bounded store.

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok, type Result } from "slang-ts";

type DeliveryStatus = {
  state: "queued" | "delivered" | "failed";
};

const checkDeliveryStatus = async (
  reference: string,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<Result<DeliveryStatus, string>> => {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    return Err("Cancelled");
  }
  await Promise.resolve(reference);
  return Ok({ state: "queued" });
};

/** Polls a delivery provider with jittered backoff, up to eight attempts. */
export const waitForDelivery = async (
  reference: string,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<Result<DeliveryStatus, string>> => {
  const delivered = await utils.retryFnWithJitter({
    fn: (attemptSignal: AbortSignal) =>
      checkDeliveryStatus(reference, attemptSignal),
    signal: signal,
    maxAttempts: 8,
    timeoutMs: 60_000,
    baseDelayMs: 1000,
    maxDelayMs: 10_000,
    jitterMs: 500,
    onResult: ({ result, retry, end, stop }) => {
      if (result.isErr) {
        return retry();
      }
      if (result.value.state === "delivered") {
        return end(result.value);
      }
      if (result.value.state === "failed") {
        return stop("Delivery failed");
      }
      return retry();
    },
  });

  return delivered;
};

type OrderSummary = {
  orderId: string;
  total: number;
};

/** Holds up to 1000 recent summaries for 30 seconds each. */
export const summaryCache = utils.createMemoryStore<OrderSummary>({
  maxKeys: 1000,
  ttlMs: 30_000,
  eviction: "lru",
});

export const rememberSummary = (summary: OrderSummary): Result<void, string> => {
  const stored = summaryCache.set({ key: summary.orderId, value: summary });
  if (stored.isErr) {
    return Err(stored.error);
  }
  return Ok(undefined);
};
```

## Helpers [#helpers]

| Helper | Use it for | Notable options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `retryFnWithJitter` | Repeating a call until its result is final | `maxAttempts` (default 10), `timeoutMs` (default 60000), `baseDelayMs`, `maxDelayMs`, `jitterMs`, `onResult`, `signal` |
| `createMemoryStore` | Bounded values with optional expiry | `maxKeys` (default 1000), `ttlMs`, `eviction` (`"reject-new"` default, or `"lru"`) |
| `dbTry` | Wrapping a database call that may throw | `message` (safe text for callers), `atFunction` |
| `describeError` | Reading a thrown error in a diagnostic log | `maxDepth`, `maxFieldLength`, `includeMessages` |
| `createRateLimiter`, `createQueue` and others | Controls and quotas | See [queues](/guide/features/queues-debounce-throttle) and [rate limiting](/guide/features/rate-limiting) |
| `resolveClientIdentity` | Reading the client address from a request | `getClientAddress`, `trustProxy` |

## Retries [#retries]

`onResult` decides what happens after each attempt. Return `retry()` to wait and try again, `end(value)` for success or `stop(message)` for a final failure. The helper returns a Result. If it runs out of attempts or time, it returns a failure with a string message.

Retry only operations that are safe to repeat. A payment or an email send needs an idempotency key before a retry is safe.

## Memory store [#memory-store]

Values are held by reference in this process. The default store rejects new keys when it is full, so an unexpected traffic spike cannot evict active values. Use LRU only when you accept evicting old entries.

`set` returns a Result. `get` returns the value or `undefined`. `consume` removes a value only when the expected value matches, which is useful for one-time tokens.

## Limits [#limits]

- Retries cannot stop code that ignores its abort signal. The helper waits for the attempt to settle.
- The store and the retry history live in memory and disappear on restart.
- `describeError` can include message text when `includeMessages` is true. Driver messages may contain data, so enable it only when you need it.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Retrying a write that is not idempotent.
- Using `dbTry` and then returning the raw error message to the client.
- Treating the memory store as shared between replicas.
- Forgetting the Result from `set`, which reports a rejected insert when the store is full.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Shared backend utilities](/guide/reference/shared-utilities) has the full reference for each helper.
- [Errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) explains failure handling in actions.
- [Queues, debounce and throttle](/guide/features/queues-debounce-throttle) covers controlled concurrency.


---

# Telemetry

Telemetry sends a span for each action or scheduled job, plus bounded metrics, to an OpenTelemetry collector. Use it when your team already reads traces and metrics in a tool such as Grafana, Honeycomb or Jaeger. Nile Js does not include a dashboard.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Enable telemetry when you need to see which actions are slow or failing across replicas, or when you want a trace from an incoming request to the action it ran. Skip it when structured file logs answer your questions.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This server creates the exporter, passes it to the execution diagnostics and sets a timeout for each execution. The collector URL and token come from your configuration module.

```ts
import { createNileServer, createNileTelemetry, createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";

const telemetry = await createNileTelemetry({
  serviceName: "shop",
  endpoint: config.telemetryEndpoint,
  headers: { authorization: "Bearer replace-with-collector-token" },
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "shop",
    description: "Storefront operations",
    actions: [],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "shop",
  services: services,
  execution: {
    timeoutMs: 15_000,
    diagnostics: {
      telemetry: telemetry,
      summaries: false,
      slowMs: 1000,
      hookTracing: false,
    },
  },
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example.com"] },
});
```

`createNileTelemetry` loads the OpenTelemetry packages only when you call it. A server that does not call it does not load them.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Where | Option | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createNileTelemetry` | `serviceName` | Name shown for this application in the collector. |
| `createNileTelemetry` | `endpoint` | OTLP HTTP base URL. Nile adds `/v1/traces` and `/v1/metrics`. |
| `createNileTelemetry` | `headers` | Headers for the collector, such as an authorization token. Read them from configuration. |
| `createNileTelemetry` | `sampleRate`, `metrics` | Sampling for traces, and whether metrics are exported. |
| `execution.diagnostics` | `telemetry` | The instance returned by `createNileTelemetry`. |
| `execution.diagnostics` | `summaries` | When true, logs a summary of successful executions. Failures and slow executions are summarized when a logger is configured. |
| `execution.diagnostics` | `slowMs` | Executions at or above this duration are reported as slow. |
| `execution.diagnostics` | `hookTracing` | Adds a span for each hook. Off by default. |

## What is recorded [#what-is-recorded]

- Spans carry the action or job name, duration, outcome and transport. Standard incoming trace headers are propagated.
- Metrics use bounded labels. Request IDs go on spans and logs, not on metric labels, so metric cardinality stays low.
- Nile does not capture payloads, tokens, raw errors or personal data. Anything you write into a log `data` object is still your responsibility.

## Limits [#limits]

- The collector is a separate service. If it is unreachable, Nile logs export errors and the action still returns its normal Result.
- Calling `telemetry.flush()` while the collector is unreachable rejects. Wrap a manual flush in `try` and `catch`, and log the failure.
- Export uses bounded buffers and deadlines, so a slow collector does not hold up requests.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Putting a collector token directly in source code. Read it from an environment variable through your configuration module.
- Expecting a Nile dashboard. Point the endpoint at a collector that your team already uses.
- Setting `hookTracing` on every service. Hook spans add volume, so enable it while you diagnose a specific action.
- Using request IDs as metric labels in your own instrumentation.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) covers the diagnostics options and log filters.
- [Logging](/guide/internals/logging) explains the file logs that telemetry complements.
- [Context and logging](/guide/features/context-and-logging) shows how execution IDs appear in logs.


---

# Validation and errors

Validation rejects a bad payload before your handler runs. A handler returns `Err` when a business rule refuses the request. Both reach the caller as a failure, so the client checks one thing: `isErr`.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Declare a Zod schema in `validation` on every action that accepts input. Use `Err` in the handler for rules that need data the schema cannot see, such as a name that is already taken or a record that belongs to another organization.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

This action validates a project and then applies a reserved-name rule in its handler. The nested `address.city` field shows how a dotted field path appears in the response.

```ts
import { createAction, createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";

const createProjectSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().trim().min(3, "Name must have at least 3 characters"),
  address: z.object({
    city: z.string().min(1, "City is required"),
  }),
  budget: z.number().int().nonnegative("Budget cannot be negative"),
});

type CreateProjectInput = z.infer<typeof createProjectSchema>;

const reservedNames: readonly string[] = ["system", "admin"];

const createProjectHandler = (input: CreateProjectInput) => {
  if (reservedNames.includes(input.name.toLowerCase())) {
    return Err("Choose a different project name");
  }

  return Ok({
    project: {
      name: input.name,
      city: input.address.city,
      budget: input.budget,
    },
  });
};

const createProjectAction = createAction<CreateProjectInput>({
  name: "create",
  description: "Create a project after validating its input",
  validation: createProjectSchema,
  handler: createProjectHandler,
});

export const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "projects",
    description: "Project operations",
    actions: [createProjectAction],
  },
]);
```

Send a payload with an empty name and an empty city:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"intent":"execute","service":"projects","action":"create","payload":{"name":"Hi","address":{"city":""},"budget":10}}'
```

The response carries the field path in `data.issues`:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Validation failed: ✖ Name must have at least 3 characters\n  → at name\n✖ City is required\n  → at address.city",
  "data": {
    "issues": [
      { "path": "name", "message": "Name must have at least 3 characters" },
      { "path": "address.city", "message": "City is required" }
    ]
  }
}
```

A rejected name returns a failure from the handler instead:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Choose a different project name",
  "data": {}
}
```

## Read failures in the client [#read-failures-in-the-client]

The frontend client returns the same Result pattern as the handler. On failure, `error` is the message and `details` holds the `data` object the server sent, including `issues` for validation failures.

```ts
const created = await nile.invoke({
  service: "projects",
  action: "create",
  payload: { name: name, address: { city: city }, budget: budget },
});

if (created.isErr) {
  console.error(created.error);
  console.error(created.details);
  return;
}

console.log(created.value);
```

Here `nile` is a client created with `createNileClient`, as in [the frontend client guide](/guide/basics/client). Read `value` only after the `isErr` check.

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Where | Option | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Action | `validation` | Zod schema for the payload. Use `null` or omit it for actions without input. |
| Action | `handler` | Named function that returns `Ok(value)` or `Err(message)`. |
| Schema | `z.infer<typeof schema>` | Input type for the handler. Use it as the generic argument to `createAction`. |

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- The order is: JWT check, global before hook, local before hooks, Zod validation, handler, local after hooks, global after hook. Before hooks see the raw payload, so validate again in them if you depend on a field.
- Zod object schemas remove keys they do not declare. The handler receives only the parsed fields.
- A validation failure returns HTTP 400 with `status: false`. Handler `Err` values also return HTTP 400.
- `data.issues` appears only for validation failures. Other failures return `data: {}`.
- A handler that throws is caught and returned as a failure with the thrown message. Return `Err` for expected cases so the message is one you chose.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Returning a plain string or throwing for an expected rule. Return `Err("...")` so the client gets a Result.
- Reading `result.value` before checking `result.isErr`.
- Putting a business rule only in the client. The server must enforce it.
- Showing `error` text from a validation failure to an end user without reading `details.issues`. The issues tell a form which field to highlight.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) explains the three response shapes.
- [Actions](/guide/basics/actions) covers action definition and naming.
- [Hooks and pipelines](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines) explains when before hooks see unvalidated input.
- [Frontend client](/guide/basics/client) covers request options and the client Result.


---

# WebSockets

Nile Js sends typed messages to connected clients over Socket.IO. You define each topic with a Zod schema, decide who may subscribe and publish, and send messages from your actions after a change commits. Your frontend receives them through `@nilejs/client`.

## When to use it [#when-to-use-it]

Use topics when a screen should update without a refresh, such as a payment status or an order timeline. Do not use topics as a queue: delivery is live only, with no stored history and no replay after a reconnect.

## Complete example [#complete-example]

The server file defines the topic, the access policies and an action that publishes after it changes a payment. Policies run for every subscription and every client publish. `authenticate` runs once per connection.

```ts
import {
  type Message,
  createAction,
  createNileServer,
  createServices,
  createTopics,
  getContext,
  type InferTopics,
} from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";

export const topics = createTopics({
  "payments.updated": {
    schema: z.object({
      paymentId: z.string(),
      status: z.enum(["pending", "paid"]),
    }),
    scope: z.object({
      organizationId: z.string(),
    }),
  },
});

export type Topics = InferTopics<typeof topics>;

const markPaidSchema = z.object({
  paymentId: z.string().min(1),
});

type MarkPaidInput = z.infer<typeof markPaidSchema>;

const markPaidHandler = async (input: MarkPaidInput) => {
  const { websocket } = getContext({ topics: topics });

  const sent = await websocket.send({
    topic: "payments.updated",
    scope: { organizationId: "org_123" },
    data: { paymentId: input.paymentId, status: "paid" },
  });

  if (sent.isErr) {
    return Err(sent.error);
  }

  return Ok({ paymentId: input.paymentId, status: "paid" });
};

const markPaidAction = createAction<MarkPaidInput>({
  name: "mark-paid",
  description: "Mark a payment as paid and notify subscribers",
  isProtected: true,
  validation: markPaidSchema,
  handler: markPaidHandler,
});

const services = createServices([
  {
    name: "payments",
    description: "Payment status",
    actions: [markPaidAction],
  },
]);

export const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "shop",
  runtime: "bun",
  native: true,
  services: services,
  auth: { secret: config.jwtSecret, method: "header" },
  websocket: {
    topics: topics,
    allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example.com"],
    authenticate: (request, auth) => {
      const token = auth.token;
      if (token === undefined || token.length === 0) {
        return Err("Missing token");
      }
      return Ok({
        session: { organizationId: "org_123", userId: "user_1" },
        expiresAt: Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000,
      });
    },
    authorizeSubscription: ({ scope, identity }) => {
      return Ok(scope.organizationId === identity.session?.organizationId);
    },
    authorizePublish: () => Ok(false),
  },
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example.com"] },
});

export const describeMessage = (
  message: Message<"payments.updated", Topics["payments.updated"]["data"]>
): string => {
  return `${message.data.paymentId} is ${message.data.status}`;
};
```

The `authenticate` callback in this example accepts any token and returns a fixed session. Replace it with real verification, as shown in [the realtime order example](/guide/examples/realtime-orders), before you deploy.

The client subscribes to one organization's scope and then calls the action over the same connection:

```ts
import { createNileSocketClient } from "@nilejs/client";
import type { Topics } from "./websockets";

interface PaymentActions {
  payments: {
    "mark-paid": { paymentId: string };
  };
}

const socket = createNileSocketClient<PaymentActions, Topics>({
  baseUrl: "https://shop.example.com",
  auth: () => ({ token: session.token }),
});

const received = await socket.receive({
  topic: "payments.updated",
  scope: { organizationId: organizationId },
  onMessage: (message) => {
    console.log(message.data.paymentId, message.data.status);
  },
});

if (received.isErr) {
  console.error(received.error);
} else {
  console.log("subscribed");
}

const marked = await socket.invoke({
  service: "payments",
  action: "mark-paid",
  payload: { paymentId: paymentId },
});

if (marked.isErr) {
  console.error(marked.error, marked.details);
}

socket.close();
```

## Options that matter [#options-that-matter]

| Option | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `topics` | Topic definitions from `createTopics`. Pass the same object to `getContext({ topics })`. |
| `allowedOrigins` | Browser origins that may connect. Other browser origins are refused. |
| `path` | Socket.IO path. Default `/socket.io`. Set it on the client too. |
| `authenticate(request, auth)` | Verifies the connection and returns an identity with `session`, `credentials` and optional `expiresAt`. |
| `authorizeSubscription` | Returns `Ok(true)` to allow a subscription. Omitting it denies subscriptions to clients. |
| `authorizePublish` | Returns `Ok(true)` to allow a client to publish. Omitting it denies client publishes. |
| `maxConnections` | Connection limit. Default 1000. |
| `authenticationTimeoutMs` | Time allowed to authenticate. Default 5000. |
| `maxMessageBytes`, `maxBufferedBytes` | Message and buffer limits. Default 1 MiB. |
| `maxConcurrentMessages`, `maxSubscriptions`, `messagesPerMinute` | Per-connection limits. Defaults 32, 100 and 600. |

## How it behaves [#how-it-behaves]

- Authentication happens once per connection. Reconnecting refreshes it and rechecks subscriptions.
- `send` on the server validates the payload against the topic schema and delivers it to subscribers whose scope matches. It does not run your client publish policy, because server code is trusted.
- A successful `send` means the message was accepted for live delivery. It does not mean every subscriber processed it.
- Send after the database write commits. A failed send does not undo the write.
- Subscriptions, connections and delivery live in one process. Multiple replicas need an application-level bridge, which Nile Js does not supply.
- A client's `receive` registers a listener. Several listeners can share one server subscription.

## Limits [#limits]

- No durable storage, replay or offline queue. A client that disconnects misses messages sent while it was away. Reload its state from an action when it reconnects.
- Protected actions called over the socket still need credentials on the connection. Put the verified headers in `credentials`.
- Scopes must be JSON values that match the topic's `scope` schema.

## Common mistakes [#common-mistakes]

- Omitting `authorizeSubscription` and wondering why subscriptions fail. Omitting a policy denies by default.
- Returning `Ok(true)` from `authorizePublish` for every client. Clients could then publish any message to any scope.
- Calling `getContext()` without `{ topics }`, which loses the topic types.
- Sending a message before the database change commits.

## Server setup on Bun [#server-setup-on-bun]

Serve the Bun socket handler with the HTTP fetch handler. Read the idle timeout from `server.websocket`:

```ts
const websocketBun = server.websocket?.bun;
if (websocketBun === undefined) {
  throw new Error("Bun socket adapter is unavailable");
}

const listener = Bun.serve({
  port: 8000,
  fetch: server.fetch,
  websocket: websocketBun,
  idleTimeout: server.websocket?.idleTimeout,
});
```

## See also [#see-also]

- [Sockets and typed messages](/guide/reference/realtime) has the complete contract, schema export and limits.
- [HTTP, WebSocket and direct calls](/guide/features/calling-actions) shows the three ways to call an action.
- [Realtime order updates example](/guide/examples/realtime-orders) runs the full flow with two organizations.

# Build with Nile

Nile Js organizes your backend into **services** and **actions**. A service groups a business domain, such as billing. An action names one operation, validates its input and runs an ordinary function. The same structure gives teammates and coding agents a path through the next feature.

## Start with one operation [#start-with-one-operation]

[Build your first service](/guide/start/getting-started), send it a request, then move the action into your application's domain structure. The complete example uses Bun native and returns a project you can inspect.

| Your next task | Guide |
| --- | --- |
| See every built-in feature with an example | [Features](/guide/features) |
| Build a complete feature step by step | [Examples](/guide/examples) |
| Find a home for growing business logic | [Application structure](/guide/start/application-structure) |
| Validate input and return useful failures | [Actions](/guide/basics/actions) and [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) |
| Share resources and access policies | [Context](/guide/basics/context) and [authentication](/guide/basics/auth) |
| Connect your frontend | [Frontend client](/guide/basics/client) |
| Add live updates | [Sockets and typed messages](/guide/reference/realtime) |
| Schedule work and control concurrency | [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations) |
| Trace a failed operation | [Logging](/guide/internals/logging) |
| Use the handler context, hooks and execution options | [Advanced](/guide/advanced) |

## Keep the business logic yours [#keep-the-business-logic-yours]

Use ordinary TypeScript functions for domain rules and your chosen library for data access. Nile Js supplies the shared execution patterns: validation, Results, hooks, context and logging. Register your services explicitly so someone joining the project can see which operations it exposes.

Choose [Bun native or the Hono adapter](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) for HTTP. Call the same action through `server.invoke` within your backend, or expose it over Socket.IO when your application needs a connected client.

## Work with a coding assistant [#work-with-a-coding-assistant]

Give your assistant the [Nile Js skill](/guide/agents/skill) and the [documentation index](/guide/reference/llms-txt), and expose selected runtime schemas through [discovery](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents). Documentation explains Nile Js conventions; your application's schemas describe its operations and input shapes. [Build with AI agents](/guide/agents) walks through the setup.


---

# CORS

CORS controls which browser origins may read responses. Configure it once for the application, then override it only where an operation needs a different policy. It does not prevent non-browser callers from invoking an action and must not replace authorization.

## Application policy [#application-policy]

For either HTTP adapter, place CORS settings under `rest`:

```ts
rest: {
  baseUrl: "/api",
  allowedOrigins: ["https://office.example.com"],
  cors: {
    defaults: {
      credentials: true,
      allowHeaders: ["Content-Type", "Authorization"],
      allowMethods: ["POST", "OPTIONS"],
    },
  },
}
```

Use explicit trusted origins when credentials are involved. Disabling CORS with `cors: { enabled: false }` skips CORS processing and callbacks; it does not make an endpoint private.

## Action-level policy [#action-level-policy]

Static action policies work with both adapters:

```ts
import { createAction } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Ok } from "slang-ts";

const readReportHandler = () => {
  return Ok({ available: true });
};

const readReport = createAction({
  name: "read",
  description: "Read a report",
  cors: { origin: "https://office.example.com" },
  handler: readReportHandler,
});
```

Set `cors: false` on an action to omit its actual-response CORS headers. `cors: true` inherits the application policy. Static policies are prepared at setup; recreate the transport after changing them.

## Native callbacks [#native-callbacks]

Bun native callbacks receive `NativeRequestContext`. Define native-specific action policies through the server map:

```ts
rest: {
  baseUrl: "/api",
  allowedOrigins: ["https://office.example.com"],
  cors: {
    actions: {
      reports: {
        read: {
          origin: (origin, context) =>
            context.request.headers.has("X-Partner") ? origin : null,
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

This example demonstrates header access, not a secure partner identity check. Validate actual credentials through authentication/authorization.

Native map entries take precedence over legacy action policies. Hono callbacks use `context.req`; they must be migrated before enabling native transport. Unsupported legacy callbacks fail at setup when CORS is enabled.

## Shared preflight [#shared-preflight]

All actions share the action endpoint. An OPTIONS preflight has no JSON action body, so it cannot choose an action-specific policy. The endpoint-level preflight must permit the origins, methods and headers required by intended action calls. The selected action’s policy then applies to the actual response.

Hono also supports path rules through `cors.addCors`; native supports equivalent rules with native callback types. See [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) and [HTTP transport](/guide/internals/rest) before migrating middleware or custom routes.


---

# Model helpers

Use `createModel` when a Drizzle-backed domain needs familiar CRUD operations. Keep custom business queries in ordinary model functions rather than forcing every operation through a generic helper.

## Create a model [#create-a-model]

This example assumes your application already defines the Drizzle table and database client; it does not create or migrate a database.

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { db } from "../client";
import { projects } from "../schema";

export const projectModel = utils.createModel(projects, {
  name: "project",
  db,
});
```

The table must be a real Drizzle table, not a plain object or a relation definition. Row/insert types come from that table. `name` supplies readable error attribution. `cursorColumn` defaults to `id`.

Omit `db` to resolve `resources.database` from the current Nile context at method-call time. This is shared application-resource access, not an automatically created per-request database connection. Missing configuration throws when a method needs the database.

## Reuse the table schemas [#reuse-the-table-schemas]

Use `utils.getZodSchema` when a custom model function needs the same insert, update and select schemas. This fragment uses the `projects` table and `utils` import from the model example above:

```ts
const projectSchemas = utils.getZodSchema(projects);
const checked = projectSchemas.insert.safeParse({ name: "Customer portal" });
```

Check `checked.success` before reading `checked.data`. A model also exposes its schemas at `projectModel.schemas`, so actions and custom data functions can share the table contract.

## Methods [#methods]

| Method | Result data |
| --- | --- |
| `create({ data, dbx? })` | Inserted row. |
| `findById(id)` | Matching row; missing data returns an Err. |
| `update({ id, data, dbx? })` | Updated row; missing data returns an Err. |
| `delete(id)` | Deleted row; missing data returns an Err. |
| `findAll()` | Rows, including an empty array when no rows exist. |
| `findPaginated({ limit?, offset? })` | `{ items, total, hasMore }`. |
| `findPaginated({ limit?, cursor, cursorColumn? })` | `{ items, nextCursor, hasMore }`. |

Ordinary methods return `Promise<Result<T, string>>`. `create` and `update` check their data against the generated insert/update schemas, then execute their queries. They validate the supplied data; they do not substitute the schema’s transformed output into the write.

Pagination defaults to 50 items. Offset mode is selected without a cursor. Cursor mode uses descending order and a less-than comparison on the selected column, fetching an extra row to detect another page. Choose a suitable stable cursor for your data; the helper does not add a multi-column tie-breaker automatically.

`findAll` and offset pagination use `created_at`, then `createdAt`, for descending ordering when present. Otherwise no default ordering is applied.

## Transaction variants [#transaction-variants]

`createTx` and `updateTx` wrap the corresponding method with `createTransactionVariant`. Pass `dbx` explicitly when a transaction is required. The wrapper calls `dbx.transaction(...)` when the supplied handle exposes it. A Drizzle transaction can expose the same method for a nested transaction or savepoint. Other handles are passed directly to the operation. Omitting `dbx` does not automatically start a transaction from the model’s configured `db`.

An Err from a transaction-wrapped operation is thrown as an Error to trigger rollback. This is a rejection boundary, not a guaranteed Result return. Guard the entire call with `safeTry` when needed. See the [data access overview](/guide/internals/db/) before composing multi-write workflows.

## Extend ordinary behavior [#extend-ordinary-behavior]

The returned object exposes `table` and `schemas.insert/update/select`. Use these with your chosen Drizzle client for joins, reports and application-specific queries. Keep those functions in the same domain’s model/repository module so the team can find them.

Queries pass through `utils.dbTry`, which keeps bounded driver cause metadata in diagnostics and returns a safe failure with a log reference when available. Model query and validation failures use `utils.handleError`, which resolves the current logger and returns an Err with its log reference. Configure a logger or supply an application policy for failures. The helper throws when required logging/database configuration is missing.

## Keep the action focused [#keep-the-action-focused]

Let actions validate their API input, enforce access policy and call a model function. Return or deliberately shape its Result rather than hiding failure branches. That keeps the operation readable as the service grows.

Continue with [application structure](/guide/start/application-structure), [context](/guide/basics/context) and [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results).


---

# Data access

Keep business operations easy to follow: an action handles its input and application policy, an ordinary domain function implements the rule, and a model/repository owns data access. This is a useful convention, not a runtime restriction. Nile does not require a particular ORM or database.

The [application structure guide](/guide/start/application-structure) shows how these modules fit together as the operation count grows.

## Bring your application’s data resource [#bring-your-applications-data-resource]

Create and configure a database client with your chosen library. Pass the existing client through `resources.database` if handlers or models should resolve it from Nile context. Connection management, credentials, migrations, indexes and deployment remain application responsibilities.

You can instead pass dependencies directly to your functions. A repository does not need to import Nile merely to be callable from an action.

## Optional Drizzle helpers [#optional-drizzle-helpers]

Access the Drizzle helpers through `import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile"`:

| Helper | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `utils.createModel` | Basic CRUD methods, validation and pagination around a table. |
| `utils.getZodSchema` | Insert, update and select Zod schemas from a real Drizzle table. |
| `utils.createTransactionVariant` | Run a Result-returning function with explicit transaction/rollback behavior. |
| `DBX<TDB>`, `DBParams<TDB>` | Describe a database or transaction dependency. |
| `utils.handleError` | Log an investigable failure and return an Err. |

Install and configure the relevant Drizzle packages/driver in your application before choosing these helpers. They do not provision a database or run migrations.

## What stays in your application [#what-stays-in-your-application]

Use ordinary functions for joins, reporting, multi-model business rules and external integrations. `createModel` exposes its table and schemas for extending common CRUD behavior; it is not a complete repository abstraction for every domain.

For multi-step writes, decide transaction boundaries explicitly. Calling several actions or attaching an after hook does not make the work atomic. A noncritical notification failure may be acceptable; a partially applied financial operation may not be. That policy belongs beside the business operation.

## Failure boundaries [#failure-boundaries]

Expected missing data can return `Err`. Driver failures should be guarded with `safeTry` and handled according to the operation. `handleError` needs a configured or explicit logger and throws if one is absent. Missing database configuration also fails rather than silently continuing.

`createTransactionVariant` deliberately throws when the wrapped function returns an Err so a database transaction can roll back. It does not convert the rejection back into an Err. Guard the whole transaction call with `safeTry` when the caller needs a Result. If no `dbx` is supplied, the wrapper calls the function without starting a transaction and still throws on Err. Supply a root database with a `transaction` method when a new transaction is required; an existing Drizzle transaction can create a nested transaction or savepoint when it exposes the same method.

See [createModel](/guide/internals/db/create-model) for the exact method boundaries, and [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) for application error handling.


---

# Engine

The engine gives every business operation the same execution path. A team can review input checks, reusable policy and the handler without learning a different convention for each service.

## Registration [#registration]

`createNileServer` creates an engine from the supplied services. Registration builds action lookups and bound executors once, records service/action counts and rejects duplicate service names or duplicate action names within a service.

Registered names identify operations. Keep meaningful domain names and action names; the engine does not infer folder structure or discover source files automatically.

## Execution order [#execution-order]

For a successful action, the order is:

1. Configured JWT authentication for a protected action.
2. Global before hook.
3. Action before hooks, sequentially.
4. Action input validation, when supplied.
5. The action handler.
6. Action after hooks, sequentially.
7. Global after hook.

An error stops the relevant pipeline unless an action hook is explicitly noncritical. After hooks run after a successful handler; they are not a `finally` block. Referenced hook actions execute their handler, not recursively their full configured pipeline.

Before hooks run before the main action’s validation. Treat their incoming data as untrusted. The global before hook’s successful return is a continuation signal; action before-hook results form the payload passed to the next action hook and validation.

See [hooks and pipelines](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines) for practical examples and failure policies.

## State boundaries [#state-boundaries]

Each action execution gets isolated hook state. Hooks for that execution can share `context.hookContext.state`, including under concurrent or nested action calls. Request sessions hold the request’s identity. Neither provides persistence between requests.

Application resources and general context keys remain shared. Put a database client or logger there; do not put the current user or per-request mutable data in a global key. See [context](/guide/basics/context).

## Calling the engine directly [#calling-the-engine-directly]

Inside an application with a configured server and context:

```ts
const result = await server.engine.executeAction(
  "projects",
  "create",
  { name: "Customer portal" },
  server.context,
);

if (result.isErr) {
  console.error(result.error);
}
```

Direct execution bypasses HTTP parsing, CORS, transport middleware and rate limits. Authentication for protected actions still depends on configured authentication and a suitable request/session context. It is not a shortcut around access policy.

Use ordinary domain functions when composition does not need another action pipeline.

## Measuring registration [#measuring-registration]

`server.engine.stats()` returns service/action registration counts and timing. `server.stats()` also includes startup duration. These are startup snapshots, not live throughput or request latency metrics. See [server setup](/guide/internals/server) and [recorded performance](/guide/reference/performance).


---

# Logging

A consistent log format helps a small team follow a failure back to the operation that produced it. Nile includes a structured logger; supply it through resources so actions, hooks and error helpers can use the same convention.

## Configure a logger [#configure-a-logger]

```ts
import { createLogger, createNileServer } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { services } from "./services";

const logger = createLogger("back-office", {
  mode: "prod",
  chunking: "daily",
});

const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "Back Office",
  services,
  resources: { logger },
});

logger.info({
  atFunction: "startup",
  message: "Application registered",
  data: { actions: server.stats().totalActions },
});
```

`createLogger` binds an application name and exposes `info`, `warn` and `error`. Each entry includes the application, function, message, optional data, level, time and a log ID.

## Choose output deliberately [#choose-output-deliberately]

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `dev` | Writes readable records to the console; returns a console-oriented marker. |
| `prod` | Writes structured records through Pino to local log files; returns the log ID. |
| `agentic` | Returns a JSON record string for the caller to consume; it is not an agent integration or persistent log sink. |

Files are written under `logs/` relative to the working directory. With no chunking, the path is `logs/{appName}.log`. Daily, weekly and monthly chunking split files under an application subdirectory.

Time-based chunking does not delete old logs, ship them to another system or provide a retention policy. Configure storage, collection and retention for your deployment. Avoid recording credentials, sensitive payloads or personal data unnecessarily.

## Return a failure with log context [#return-a-failure-with-log-context]

For an expected business refusal, `Err("Project is archived")` may be enough. For a failure that needs investigation, `handleError` logs through an explicit logger or the current Nile resource and returns an Err:

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";

const failure = utils.handleError({
  logger,
  atFunction: "projects.create",
  message: "Could not save the project",
  data: { operation: "insert-project" },
});
```

The returned message includes the logger’s returned identifier. In production mode this can be used to locate the corresponding record. `handleError` throws if no logger is available: missing logging configuration should be fixed rather than silently ignored.

Inside an HTTP request, direct action call or scheduled execution, Nile’s logger automatically includes the active `requestId` and any `traceId`, `spanId` or `runId`. Startup logs have no execution to attach. Plain `console.log` calls and arbitrary third-party loggers do not receive this metadata.

Use `requestId`, `runId` and `traceId` in `getLogs` filters to follow related records. Failures and slow executions receive diagnostic summaries when a logger is configured; successful summaries are opt-in. For a hosted destination, configure [telemetry](/guide/reference/operations#read-logs-then-add-a-destination-when-useful). Nile exports traces and metrics through OTLP while file logs remain available.

## Read local records [#read-local-records]

```ts
import { getLogs } from "@nilejs/nile";

const errors = getLogs(
  { appName: "back-office", level: "error" },
  { chunking: "daily" },
);
```

Use the same chunking strategy as the writer. Filters include application name, log ID, level and date range. Reading local files is useful for inspection; it is not a substitute for deployment-wide observability.

Continue with [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) and [hooks](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines).


---

# REST

Nile exposes registered business operations through `POST {baseUrl}/services`. The transport parses input, applies configured HTTP policies and sends an operation to the engine. The same action organization works with Bun native and the Hono adapter.

## Request and response [#request-and-response]

With `rest.baseUrl: "/api"`:

```http
POST /api/services
Content-Type: application/json
```

```json
{
  "intent": "execute",
  "service": "projects",
  "action": "create",
  "payload": { "name": "Customer portal" }
}
```

A successful execution uses an HTTP 200 envelope containing `status: true`, a message and action data. Action failures use a failed envelope and HTTP 400. Invalid transport input, disabled discovery, upload violations, missing routes and unexpected HTTP errors have their own status codes. Do not treat every non-200 response as a business Result.

See [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) for the handler, HTTP and client boundaries.

## Intents [#intents]

| Intent | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `execute` | Invoke a registered operation. |
| `explore` | Inspect visible services/actions when discovery is enabled. |
| `schema` | Retrieve supported input schemas as JSON Schema when enabled. |

Discovery is disabled by default. Enable it deliberately and consider a discovery secret. Schema conversions are lazy and cached; action outputs are not cached. See [discovery and agents](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents).

## Configure the boundary [#configure-the-boundary]

Settings remain under `rest` for both adapters:

| Setting | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `baseUrl` | Prefix for the action endpoint. |
| `allowedOrigins`, `cors` | Browser cross-origin policy. |
| `rateLimiting` | Configured request limit and client-key source. |
| `uploads` | Multipart validation and limits. |
| `enableStatic`, `staticDir` | Optional static serving under `/assets/*`. |
| `enableStatus` | Optional `GET /status` health response. |
| `discovery` | Explicit runtime metadata/schema access. |
| `diagnostics` | Diagnostic output for transport work. |

Rate limiting is enabled when a limiting header is configured. In-memory limits are local to a process; choose a suitable shared store for multiple instances. Trust forwarded client headers only behind infrastructure that controls them. CORS is browser policy, not authentication or authorization.

Multipart requests carry `intent`, `service` and `action` fields alongside their fields/files. See [uploads](/guide/basics/uploads) for actual payload shapes and limits.

## Native middleware and routes [#native-middleware-and-routes]

After creating a Bun-native server:

```ts
const native = server.nativeRest;
if (!native) {
  throw new Error("Native transport was not initialized");
}

native.addMiddleware("/api", async (context, next) => {
  context.setHeader("X-Application", "back-office");
  await next();
});

native.route("GET", "/health", (context) => {
  return context.json({ ready: true });
});
```

Native middleware can return a Response to stop execution or await `next()` and modify response headers. Native request state uses `context.get/set`; request headers are read through `context.request.headers`.

## Hono compatibility [#hono-compatibility]

Existing applications keep `server.rest.app` for Hono routes and `server.rest.addMiddleware` for action middleware. Hono callbacks receive a Hono Context, not a native context. Migrate those callbacks when changing adapters; setting `native: true` does not translate Hono plugins.

See [custom routes](/guide/basics/custom-routes), [CORS](/guide/internals/cors) and [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters).

## Put a bound on repeated requests [#put-a-bound-on-repeated-requests]

When an application needs a request quota, configure it alongside the transport rather than repeating a counter in each action. This server-config fragment applies a per-client limit:

```ts
rest: {
  baseUrl: "/api",
  allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
  rateLimiting: {
    limitingHeader: "x-forwarded-for",
    windowMs: 60_000,
    limit: 120,
    standardHeaders: true,
  },
}
```

Use a header supplied and overwritten by a trusted proxy; an arbitrary caller-controlled header is not a verified identity. Missing client information can make requests share a fallback key. Rate limiting complements authorization rather than replacing it.

The default in-memory store belongs to one process. Multiple instances need a deliberately chosen shared-store policy if they must enforce one combined quota. Native stores implement Nile's native store contract; Hono stores use the Hono rate-limiter contract. See [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) before moving an existing custom store between adapters. Application-owned stores remain responsible for external connections and lifecycle.


---

# Server

`createNileServer` registers your application, creates context and prepares the selected HTTP adapter. It does not start a network listener. This keeps application setup separate from deployment.

## Bun native [#bun-native]

```ts
import { createNileServer } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { services } from "./services";

const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "Back Office",
  services,
  runtime: "bun",
  native: true,
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    allowedOrigins: ["https://office.example.com"],
    enableStatus: true,
  },
});

const native = server.nativeRest;
if (!native) {
  throw new Error("Native transport was not initialized");
}

Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: native.fetch });
```

Bun native requires explicit `runtime: "bun"`. Pass `server.nativeRest.fetch` to `Bun.serve`, as above. Applications that omit `native` use the Hono handler, `server.rest.app.fetch`, instead. See [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) for listeners and migration differences.

## Shared resources [#shared-resources]

Supply your application’s logger, database client or other long-lived resources through `resources`. Handlers and hooks receive the same application context. Nile does not open your database connection or manage its lifecycle.

Keep per-request identity in request sessions and action-specific values in hook state. General `context.set` keys are shared across requests. See [context](/guide/basics/context) and [logging](/guide/internals/logging).

## Startup work [#startup-work]

`onBoot.fn` receives context and returns `Ok(null)` or a failed Result. The default maximum wait is 10,000 ms; customize `onBoot.maxWaitTime` when necessary. Missing required configuration, failed boot work and duplicate registration are setup failures, not user input errors.

Nile reuses its existing instance unless `forceNewInstance: true` is set. Use that option deliberately when creating isolated instances, for example in tests.

## Understand what loaded [#understand-what-loaded]

Nile prints service/action registration statistics by default. Disable that output with `logServices: false` and inspect the same startup measurements yourself:

```ts
console.log(server.stats());
```

The returned snapshot contains:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `totalServices` | Number of registered services. |
| `totalActions` | Number of registered actions. |
| `registrationDurationMs` | Engine registration time. |
| `startupDurationMs` | Framework startup, including awaited boot work. |
| `services` | Each service’s name, description, action count and `registrationDurationMs`. |

These timings help explain startup work as your application grows. They do not measure live requests, imported module initialization before the factory call, database latency or production capacity.

## Add policy where the team can find it [#add-policy-where-the-team-can-find-it]

Global before/after hooks receive the application context and action metadata. Action hooks can compose reusable registered handlers with critical/noncritical failure behavior. Configure authentication explicitly and implement your application’s authorization rules. See [authentication](/guide/basics/auth) and [hooks](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines).


---

# FAQ

## Who is Nile for? [#who-is-nile-for]

Small teams building growing business applications: internal tools, dashboards, billing systems and product backends. A few conventions give each operation a recognizable home, so adding another feature does not require inventing another application structure.

The maintainer uses Nile for a fintech backend with over 500 actions, an internal Back Office shipped in days, and Wi-Fi billing receiving thousands of requests a day. These are in-house accounts, not independent performance or delivery guarantees.

## Does Nile require domain-driven design? [#does-nile-require-domain-driven-design]

Nile groups actions into services. Organizing those services around business domains makes the application easier to navigate, but Nile does not impose domain aggregates, repositories or a particular folder tree. Ordinary functions can contain business rules; only operations exposed through the action API need to become actions.

Start with the [application structure guide](/guide/start/application-structure).

## How are actions addressed? [#how-are-actions-addressed]

Send `POST /api/services` when `rest.baseUrl` is `/api`. The body identifies the operation:

```json
{
  "intent": "execute",
  "service": "projects",
  "action": "create",
  "payload": { "name": "Customer portal" }
}
```

Nile registers named operations at startup and resolves them through precomputed lookups. This keeps dispatch independent of scanning the entire action collection. Parsing, validation, hooks, business logic and response serialization still take time; constant-time lookup does not imply constant request cost or guaranteed throughput.

Use meaningful operation names and register each action in its service. [Custom routes](/guide/basics/custom-routes) remain available for webhooks, health checks and other HTTP needs.

## What happens when an action fails? [#what-happens-when-an-action-fails]

Return `Err(message)` for an expected failure and `Ok(data)` for success. Guarded handler execution converts unexpected handler failures into a failed Result. HTTP responses use a `status`, `message`, `data` envelope; the client exposes its own response shape.

Startup configuration errors can throw, and transport errors can return HTTP 500. The Result convention does not make applications crash-proof. See [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results).

## Does Nile handle access control? [#does-nile-handle-access-control]

Nile can verify JWTs for protected actions when server authentication is configured. Your application implements role, organization and resource policies through hooks or business logic. `accessControl` metadata alone does not enforce a policy. [Authentication](/guide/basics/auth) explains the boundary.

## Are sessions persistent? [#are-sessions-persistent]

No. Request sessions carry identity/state within the current request. They are not a cross-request session database. Persist workflow progress in your application’s chosen storage and load it explicitly when needed.

## How does the frontend connect? [#how-does-the-frontend-connect]

Use `@nilejs/client` to invoke named actions. The CLI can generate service/action input types from the local service registry using Bun. This checks operation names and payloads when supplied to the client; it does not automatically infer server return types end to end. See the [client guide](/guide/basics/client).

## Can agents discover and execute operations? [#can-agents-discover-and-execute-operations]

When explicitly enabled, `explore` and `schema` expose operation metadata and supported input schemas. An agent integration still needs to select permitted tools, supply credentials, validate its inputs and invoke actions. Discovery is disabled by default. Nile does not ship an MCP server or universal model adapter.

Predictable code organization also helps coding agents navigate an application. That is separate from runtime discovery. See [discovery and agents](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents).

## What is cached? [#what-is-cached]

JSON Schema conversions are performed on demand and cached by default. Action results are not automatically cached. Your application owns data caches, invalidation and any persistent state. Discovery cache controls are documented in the discovery guide.

## Must I use Bun, Hono or Drizzle? [#must-i-use-bun-hono-or-drizzle]

Choose Bun native explicitly with `runtime: "bun", native: true`. Existing applications retain the Hono adapter by default; it supports Bun and Node. Their middleware and request-context APIs differ.

Choose your own database and data-access modules. Nile’s Drizzle helpers are optional. Read [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) and [data access](/guide/internals/db/).

## What about performance and future features? [#what-about-performance-and-future-features]

The [performance page](/guide/reference/performance) includes recorded measurements, methodology and reproducible sources. They describe a specific workload and machine. Follow [repository issues](https://github.com/nile-js/nile/issues) for current discussion.


---

# Choosing Nile

Choose Nile when a small team wants a consistent place for growing business operations, while keeping its business logic in ordinary TypeScript functions.

A service groups related actions. Each action names an operation, can validate its input and returns an explicit Result. Shared context and hooks let the team apply dependencies and policies consistently. Learn one operation’s shape, then follow the same path through the next domain.

## Decide from the work you need to do [#decide-from-the-work-you-need-to-do]

| What matters to your team | What Nile offers | What to consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finding and extending existing behavior | Services and named actions organized around domains | Your team still chooses useful boundaries and names. |
| Keeping failure paths understandable | `Ok`/`Err`, guarded handlers and configured error logging | Decide which failures are expected and what information is safe to expose. |
| Sharing policies across operations | Global hooks and action-level pipelines | Authorization policy is application code, not an automatic interpretation of metadata. |
| Keeping frontend calls consistent | A fetch-based client and generated input types | Output types are not automatically inferred from handlers. |
| Letting tools inspect operations | Opt-in discovery and JSON Schema export | Tool adapters, credentials and permissions remain your responsibility. |
| Using existing libraries | Resources supplied through context and ordinary modules | Nile does not provision infrastructure or manage your database lifecycle. |

## Compare programming models, not checkmarks [#compare-programming-models-not-checkmarks]

[Elysia](https://elysiajs.com/), [Hono](https://hono.dev/), [Fastify](https://fastify.dev/) and [Express](https://expressjs.com/) are worth evaluating when HTTP route design is central to your application. Nile’s action interface addresses business operations through one configured POST endpoint. Custom routes provide an escape hatch; they do not turn each action into an independently cacheable GET resource.

[tRPC](https://trpc.io/) is worth evaluating when inferred server/client types are a primary requirement. Nile uses a different flow: optional runtime schema discovery, CLI-generated input types and a client that accepts those types. Do not assume a monorepo is required by tRPC or that Nile provides the same return-type inference.

[NestJS](https://nestjs.com/), [AdonisJS](https://adonisjs.com/) and [Encore](https://encore.dev/ts) offer their own application conventions and tooling. [Effect](https://effect.website/) has its own model for errors, dependencies and execution. Evaluate those models against how your team wants to work. Nile’s particular choice is a functional service/action structure with a small set of common execution patterns.

For flexible consumer-defined data queries, evaluate whether a GraphQL API fits better than a named operation interface.

## The constraints to understand [#the-constraints-to-understand]

- Services and actions are registered at startup. Nile is not a dynamic plugin registry.
- Built-in action input validation uses Zod. Keep the handler’s declared input type aligned with its schema.
- Expected failures use Results, but invalid setup and some lower-level utilities can throw.
- Discovery is off by default. It helps build tool integrations; it does not provide an agent runtime.
- Direct calls and WebSocket action calls share the engine with HTTP. See [production operations](/guide/reference/operations) for transport setup, lifecycle, scheduling and observability. Use typed Socket.IO topics for live subscriptions. Custom HTTP routes can return streaming responses.
- General context keys and resources are shared. Request sessions and action hook state are isolated; they are not persistent storage.

## Try a representative operation [#try-a-representative-operation]

Build something your team actually needs: create a project, approve a request or change a billing plan. Follow it from input to policy, business function, data access and frontend call. That shows the practical fit more clearly than a feature inventory.

Start with [application structure](/guide/start/application-structure), then review [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results), [hooks](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines) and [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters).

The [recorded benchmark](/guide/reference/performance) supports a separate performance discussion. It does not establish a universal winner or replace choosing an architecture your team can maintain.


---

[Read the full documentation bundle](/llms-full.txt)
