# Coding assistants

Nile Js's [llms.txt](/llms.txt) lists the public guides, and [llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt) contains the documentation bundle. Use them to give a coding assistant the current service/action conventions, runtime APIs and examples before it changes an application.

The npm package also includes `SKILL.md` and these generated documentation files under `docs/`. Follow the application's own instructions and check its existing service registry before adding another operation.

Nile is listed on [Context7](https://context7.com/nile-js/nile). If your assistant has Context7 configured, it can retrieve library documentation through that integration. Availability and retrieved versions depend on that service and your assistant setup.

Documentation access is separate from [runtime API discovery](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents). Reading these files does not give an agent credentials or permission to execute an application's actions.


---

# Running Nile in production

Nile keeps business operations in services and actions. HTTP, direct calls and WebSockets use the same engine. Schedules and function controls support background work without requiring a second application architecture.

## Call actions without HTTP [#call-actions-without-http]

```ts
const result = await server.invoke({
  service: "orders",
  action: "create",
  payload: { name: "First order" },
});
if (result.isErr) {
  return result;
}
```

This executes normal hooks, validation and configured authentication. `visibility.rpc: false` disables direct access. Backend code can supply `session`, `credentials`, `signal`, `requestId` and `clientKey`. Session data does not bypass configured JWT verification; use `credentials` for it. Nested calls inherit cancellation and correlation, but receive isolated session containers and action state. Use `context.execution` for the current ID, transport, signal and optional trace IDs. `getContext()` resolves the active execution's instance.

`rpc.enabled: false` disables the direct interface. It creates no listener or separate wire protocol; the supported API is `server.invoke`. An MCP integration can use it; a built-in MCP server is not included.

## HTTP and sockets together [#http-and-sockets-together]

Socket.IO supplies Nile’s websocket interface. Configure topics, authentication and access policies under websocket; use the dedicated client’s invoke/send/receive methods. REST and sockets share the action pipeline and listener. See [Actions and messages over Socket.IO](/guide/reference/realtime) for typed contracts, Bun/Node setup, limits, delivery semantics and schema export.

## Deploy and shut down predictably [#deploy-and-shut-down-predictably]

`server.lifecycle` exposes `state()`, `isReady()`, `active()`, `register()` and `shutdown()`. Initialization completes before schedules start. With `rest.enableStatus`, `/status` is the existing health endpoint and `/ready` reports readiness.

```ts
const report = await server.lifecycle.shutdown({ timeoutMs: 10_000 });
```

Shutdown rejects new work, stops schedule admission, drains accepted executions and registered resources, then closes resources. Repeated calls share the same shutdown operation. A deadline requests cancellation; JavaScript work ignoring cancellation cannot be forcibly stopped. The report includes `timedOut`, cleanup `errors` and `remainingExecutions`.

Register resources with `name`, optional `stop`, `drain` and `close(signal)` callbacks. A stop callback should stop admission promptly, not wait for connections that need a later close phase. Application-specific database cleanup belongs in the application's callback. Nile does not install global signal handlers; connect your deployment's shutdown signal to this API. Boot failures reject startup after cleanup rather than terminating an embedding process.

## Limit requests and cancel work [#limit-requests-and-cancel-work]

HTTP protection accepts `rest.protection.maxBodyBytes` (default 10 MiB; `false` disables it). Nile checks actual bytes, including bodies with missing or inaccurate Content-Length, before JSON/form parsing. This buffers the bounded request body; configure a suitable limit for uploads or implement a custom streaming route outside this parser.

Set `rest.protection.getClientAddress` to return the peer address from your listener, never from a request header. Set `rest.protection.trustProxy` to return `true` only for proxy addresses you operate. Nile reads `x-forwarded-for` only when the actual peer is trusted, and it ignores other forwarded headers by default. `utils.resolveClientIdentity(request, protection)` returns the resolved `address`, `peer` and `source`. The legacy rate-limiting header (`rest.rateLimiting.limitingHeader`) remains application-controlled; do not treat a client-chosen header as verified identity.

`execution.timeoutMs` requests cancellation and returns a timeout failure to the caller. Handlers can pass `context.execution.signal` to compatible dependencies. Timed-out work stays tracked until it actually finishes. Cancellation does not roll back writes or interrupt code that ignores the signal.

## Read logs, then add a destination when useful [#read-logs-then-add-a-destination-when-useful]

Nile's logger keeps structured file output and readable development output. Execution IDs are attached to related logs automatically. Existing error/log IDs remain separate. `getLogs` accepts `requestId`, `runId` and `traceId` filters. Reused asynchronous file writers expose `flush` and `close` through `createLogger`; the lifecycle manages these when that logger is supplied as a resource.

```ts
const telemetry = await createNileTelemetry({
  serviceName: "shop",
  endpoint: config.observability.endpoint,
  headers: config.observability.headers,
});

// Inside createNileServer configuration:
execution: {
  diagnostics: {
    telemetry,
    summaries: false,
    slowMs: 1000,
    hookTracing: false,
  },
}
```

The destination is an OTLP HTTP base URL; Nile adds `/v1/traces` and `/v1/metrics`. Configure credentials through your application's configuration. No destination is needed to keep file logs. SDK/exporter code loads only when `createNileTelemetry` is called.

Action/job names, duration, outcome and transport produce traces and bounded-cardinality metrics. Request IDs belong on spans/logs, not metric labels. Standard incoming trace context is propagated. Hooks get detailed spans only when requested. Nile does not automatically capture payloads, tokens, raw errors or personal data. Application-written log data remains the application's responsibility.

Failures and slow executions are summarized when a logger is configured; successful summaries are opt-in. OpenTelemetry supplies implementation plumbing, not a viewer: your existing frontend can continue reading structured logs, while the configured destination stores and displays exported data. This integration does not require a Nile-hosted dashboard. Advanced exporters, metric providers, trace sampling and disabling metrics are available. SDK buffers/export deadlines are bounded, and shutdown flushes owned providers. An externally supplied metric provider remains application-owned.

## Schedule business work [#schedule-business-work]

```ts
import type { JobRunContext, JobRunEvent, SchedulerOptions } from "@nilejs/nile";

const billingSummaryJob = async (run: JobRunContext) => {
  return await buildBillingSummary({ signal: run.signal });
};

const recordRunEvent = async (event: JobRunEvent) => {
  await recordJobEvent(event);
};

export const schedules: SchedulerOptions = {
  jobs: [
    {
      name: "billing-summary",
      schedule: {
        weekly: "monday",
        at: "09:00",
        timezone: "Africa/Kampala",
      },
      handler: billingSummaryJob,
    },
  ],
  onRunEvent: recordRunEvent,
};
```

Pass `schedules` to `createNileServer`. `recordJobEvent` and `buildBillingSummary` above are application functions. The recorder receives started/completed/failed/skipped events, job/run IDs, timestamps and completion duration. Handler return values and raw errors are not persisted automatically. Recorder failures do not fail business work; `onRecorderError(job)` can report persistence trouble. Recorder capacity and timeout are bounded; stalled writers retain their capacity slot until they settle.

Schedules support:

- `{ midnight: true, timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }`
- `{ daily: true, at: "09:00", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }`
- `{ weekly: "monday", at: "09:00", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }`
- `{ cron: "0 9 * * 1-5", timezone: "Africa/Kampala" }`
- `{ once: "2027-01-01T09:00:00+03:00" }`
- `{ every: "15m" }` or a millisecond number

Calendar schedules use Croner and default to UTC. One-time string dates require an offset and must be in the future at registration. Intervals are elapsed delays after completion, so slow runs do not create a backlog. Overlap is skipped. Missed runs are not replayed. `server.scheduler` exposes `inspect`, `runNow`, `start`, `stop` and `drain`. Standalone `createScheduler` registers stopped schedules.

Schedules run in every process where enabled. Recording events does not make them durable or ensure a single execution across replicas. Use a dedicated scheduler process or an external scheduler when needed. A stopped scheduler cannot restart; create a new instance. One-time jobs are not persisted across restarts.

## Control execution with ordinary functions [#control-execution-with-ordinary-functions]

Factories return `run(input, { signal? })`, `stop()`, `drain()` and `close()`:

| Factory | Options and behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `createDebounce` | `task`, `waitMs`; execute the latest input after quiet, explicitly fail replaced callers. |
| `createThrottle` | `task`, `waitMs`, `leading` (true), `trailing` (false); optionally retain the latest trailing call. |
| `createQueue` | `task`, `concurrency` (1), pending `capacity` (1000); FIFO admission, no unbounded pending work. |
| `createBatch` | `task`, `size`, `waitMs`, `concurrency` (1), buffered `capacity` (1000); ordered per-item Results. |

Tasks receive `(input, signal)` and can return ordinary values or Results. Output denotes the final unwrapped value. A batch task returns one Result per input, in the same order. Configuration errors throw; expected closed/full/replaced/cancelled outcomes return failures. Cancellation settles a caller but keeps running work's concurrency slot until the task settles.

`utils.createGroupedControl({ key, create, maxKeys, idleMs? })` isolates controls by an explicit key. Group capacity is bounded. With `idleMs` configured, idle queues release their keys after accepted work actually settles; see [idle keyed queues](/guide/reference/shared-utilities#reclaim-idle-keyed-queues). `createControlResource(name, control)` registers stop/drain/close lifecycle behavior. Stop admission before draining. These queues and buffers are in memory and do not survive process termination.

## Share action quotas across interfaces [#share-action-quotas-across-interfaces]

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";

const limiter = utils.createRateLimiter({
  strategy: "token-bucket",
  capacity: 20,
  refillPerSecond: 5,
  cooldown: { durationMs: 1000, multiplier: 2, maxMs: 30_000 },
  maxKeys: 10_000,
});

// Inside server configuration:
execution: {
  rateLimit: {
    store: limiter,
    key: ({ context }) => context.clientKey ?? "anonymous",
  },
}
```

Policies resolve from global to service to action; the most specific overrides, and `false` disables inheritance. Configure service/action overrides under `execution.services[service].rateLimit` and `.actions[action].rateLimit`. Keys run after configured authentication and the global before hook. Use verified identities from the current context when quotas should follow users or organizations.

Strategies are fixed window (`limit`, `windowMs`), exact sliding window (`limit`, `windowMs`) and token bucket (`capacity`, `refillPerSecond`). `consume({ key, cost? })` returns a Result containing `allowed`, `remaining`, `retryAfterMs` and an optional denial reason. Cooldowns are optional; repeated denials can extend a capped escalating cooldown.

The default memory store expires inactive allowances lazily and never evicts active quotas to admit new keys. At capacity it rejects new keys. `eviction: "reject-new"` disables sweeping other keys; explicitly reset/retire keys when selecting that policy. `reset(key?)` is an operator action and restores allowances. Call `close` when the application owns the limiter's lifetime.

A shared external store must atomically check and consume the full allowance through `consume`; separate get/set operations can race. No Redis/database store is supplied. Existing HTTP rate limiting remains supported independently; enabling both layers intentionally enforces both policies.

## Project structure [#project-structure]

Nile inspects recognized source layout once during boot. Existing projects receive warnings; `project.structure` can be `"warn"`, `"error"` or `false`. New CLI projects use `"error"`. Set `project.root` to the backend package root in a monorepo. Source-less bundles skip inspection unless a root is explicitly supplied. checkProjectStructure({ root }) exposes the same Result report without starting a server.

Use `src/services/services.config.ts` and `service/actions/<action>.ts`. Larger actions can use `service/actions/<action>/<action>.ts`, `index.ts` and private `modules/`. Service-shared helpers belong in `service/modules/`. The registry stays explicit; filenames never automatically execute/register actions. Existing flat layouts remain compatible in warning mode. Action entry points above 400 lines receive refactoring guidance. Nile does not scan secrets or follow source symlinks.

The CLI generates action directories with `nile generate action <service> <action> --folder`. Schema, types and modules files should be created only when needed. No existing application is automatically moved/refactored.

## Shared backend helpers [#shared-backend-helpers]

See [Shared backend utilities](/guide/reference/shared-utilities) for safe database diagnostics, explicit jittered retries, bounded TTL storage, idle grouped queues and client-IP normalization. These helpers use the existing Slang Result conventions; retries use superPromise for cooperative deadlines and cancellable waits. Grouped controls retain keys by default; queues can opt into idle cleanup without hiding running work.


---

# Performance and methodology

A growing backend needs to do more than return hello world. This comparison runs an authenticated ecommerce workflow across 300 business operations: 50 shops with catalog, product, cart, quote, checkout and order operations.

The results below describe one recorded workload on an actively used PC. They are not maximum-throughput measurements or a universal ranking of frameworks. Choose an application structure your team can maintain, and measure your own workload before making capacity decisions.

[Chart: six-round ecommerce throughput averages with shared Zod payload validation enabled](/benchmarks/benchmark-validated.svg)

## Recorded results [#recorded-results]

All six samples per selected framework and validation mode are retained. The table uses arithmetic mean requests per second; ranges and coefficient of variation show how much the samples moved. Close averages with overlapping ranges do not establish a reliable winner.

| Framework | Average req/s | Range across six rounds | Variation (CV) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nile | 7,290 | 6,194–7,964 | 9.5% |
| Hono | 7,067 | 6,140–8,105 | 10.3% |
| Elysia | 6,797 | 3,405–8,128 | 23.6% |
| Effect | 5,343 | 4,790–5,644 | 5.7% |
| Fastify | 2,790 | 1,553–3,369 | 23.2% |
| NestJS | 2,302 | 1,068–3,067 | 32.7% |
| AdonisJS | 2,001 | 1,269–2,534 | 27.2% |
| Express | 1,729 | 940–2,376 | 36.8% |
| tRPC | 1,295 | 680–1,518 | 22.4% |
| Encore | 668 | 635–680 | 2.3% |

[Payload validation off chart](/benchmarks/benchmark-no-payload-validation.svg) · [Raw measurements](/benchmarks/results.json) · [Derived rankings and ratios](/benchmarks/rankings.json)

## What happened [#what-happened]

Each framework exposed the same business operations using its own HTTP stack. Nile addressed 300 named actions through one POST endpoint. A fresh application process handled each sample; a separate Bun process generated requests on the same machine.

Before timing, the runner checked all 300 operations, authentication rejection, payload validation, CORS behavior and state accounting. It then sent 500 practice shopping journeys, cleared their state and measured 5,000 journeys with up to 32 concurrent shoppers. Each journey made six dependent requests, checked every response and ended in an order. Final state had to contain 5,000 orders and no pending carts.

Every contender ran in each round before the next round started. The starting contender rotated, and validation-mode order alternated. Results were saved after each sample; individual slow samples were not discarded. Warmup and coordination requests were outside the measured counts.

JWT and CORS remained enabled. The two modes toggle the shared Zod payload schemas. Nile still validates its protocol envelope in both modes. Data lives in memory: no database, disk durability, external payment service or production network was measured.

## Machine and versions [#machine-and-versions]

- Intel Core i5-6300U at 2.40 GHz, four logical CPUs, about 15.5 GiB RAM.
- Bun 1.4.2 and Node 24.16.0. Framework versions, dependency pins, hashes and actual runtime details are retained in the raw results and benchmark locks.
- Recorded October 2026. Desktop applications remained active; client and application shared CPU and memory. That contention limits conclusions about small differences.
- Nile used the optimized local Bun native build. The recorded raw provenance predates its version-only bump to 1.0.0; the framework JavaScript build hash was unchanged by that bump.

## Adapter and validator choices matter [#adapter-and-validator-choices-matter]

The selected chart has one entry per framework: Nile, Hono, Elysia and Effect use Bun; Express, Fastify, NestJS with Fastify, AdonisJS and tRPC use Node; Encore uses its genuine compiled production Node/Rust image. The raw historical matrix also retains additional variants. The current reproduction runner selects these ten entries.

Shared business logic and Zod schemas keep application behavior comparable, but they do not exercise each framework's most optimized native validation path. In particular, the Encore fixture uses `api.raw`, JavaScript body parsing and Zod rather than compiled typed-endpoint validation in Rust. Elysia also uses the common Zod path. tRPC retains its native procedure and response envelopes. Common authentication uses the same JWT verifier.

These are real measurements of these particular adapters and this workflow. They do not support a claim that Nile is universally the fastest framework, or that the chart measures every framework at its best. Framework-owned hello-world or native-validator benchmarks answer a different question. Encore's [published methodology](https://encore.dev/blog/event-loops), for example, uses different validators and selects the best of five runs.

## Reproduce or inspect the comparison [#reproduce-or-inspect-the-comparison]

The [benchmark README and setup script](https://github.com/nile-js/nile/tree/main/packages/benchmarks) describe the supported Linux x64 host, locked dependencies, verified Encore compiler and real production image build. No application database is required.

From the repository root:

```sh
bun packages/benchmarks/suite/setup.mjs
bun packages/benchmarks/suite/setup.mjs --check
NODE_ENV=production bun packages/benchmarks/suite/ecommerce/full/run.mjs --smoke
NODE_ENV=production bun packages/benchmarks/suite/ecommerce/full/run.mjs --rounds=6
```

The smoke run checks behavior without timed load. A fresh six-round, ten-framework run measures 3.6 million requests plus warmup; allow ten minutes or more. Timestamped local results remain separate from these published historical measurements. The runner shuts down the servers and uniquely named containers it starts.

Generate rankings and charts using the commands in the benchmark README. Rankings reject incomplete rounds and inconsistent measured samples. The chart renderer verifies the raw source hash before rendering.

## Compared with the published package [#compared-with-the-published-package]

A separate [three-round comparison against npm 0.0.17](/benchmarks/npm-comparison.json) measured the current native build at about 1.25 times the published package's throughput without payload validation, and 1.31 times with validation. Both ran on Bun, using whole installed packages and their resolved dependencies. This is an observation on this PC, not a tenfold improvement or a code-only measurement.

Performance supports the development workflow; it does not replace application design, database planning or production load testing. Continue with [application structure](/guide/start/application-structure) to see how growing business operations stay navigable.


---

# Sockets and typed messages

Nile keeps transport configuration under rest, rpc and websocket. REST and sockets can run together; action invocations use the same validation, hooks, authentication and execution pipeline. Socket.IO provides connection handling beneath the Nile API.

## Define topic contracts [#define-topic-contracts]

```ts
import { createTopics, type InferTopics } from "@nilejs/nile";
import z from "zod";

export const topics = createTopics({
  "payments.updated": {
    schema: z.object({ paymentId: z.string(), status: z.enum(["pending", "paid"]) }),
    scope: z.object({ organizationId: z.string() }),
  },
});
export type Topics = InferTopics<typeof topics>;
```

createTopic is an optional identity helper for individual definitions. Topics without a scope schema omit scope from calls. Topic names, schema input, parsed output and scope infer from the definitions. Data and parsed scope must be JSON serializable. An emitted Message contains id, topic, data, scope and time (ISO string).

## Configure the backend [#configure-the-backend]

```ts
const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "shop",
  runtime: "bun",
  native: true,
  services,
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example"] },
  websocket: {
    topics,
    allowedOrigins: ["https://shop.example"],
    authenticate: (request, auth) => verifySocketSession({ request, auth }),
    authorizeSubscription: ({ scope, identity }) =>
      Ok(scope.organizationId === identity.session?.organizationId),
    authorizePublish: ({ scope, identity }) =>
      Ok(scope.organizationId === identity.session?.organizationId),
  },
});
```

verifySocketSession is application code returning Ok({ session, credentials?, clientKey?, expiresAt? }) or Err. Auth is a string-valued object supplied by the client at connection time; cookies are available on request. Authentication is separate from topic access. Both subscription and client publishing require explicit policies returning Ok(true). Omitting a publishing policy denies client send. Subscription never grants publishing permission. Topic policy callbacks receive an isolated socket session context. Policies must use verified identity, not a client-supplied organization alone.

Built-in JWT checking still applies when invoking protected actions. expiresAt is epoch milliseconds, checked on operations and event delivery. Reconnect refreshes authentication and rechecks subscriptions. There is no automatic durable replay.

## Backend messaging [#backend-messaging]

```ts
await server.websocket.send({
  topic: "payments.updated",
  scope: { organizationId },
  data: { paymentId, status: "paid" },
});

// Within an action, use the existing definitions to infer the scoped context.
const { websocket } = getContext({ topics: topics });
const sent = await websocket.send({
  topic: "payments.updated",
  scope: { organizationId },
  data: { paymentId, status: "paid" },
});
if (sent.isErr) {
  return sent;
}
```

getContext({ topics }) infers from the actual definitions and verifies that they belong to the active Nile instance. No repeated payload interface or type cast is needed. Existing getContext<TDB>() remains supported. server.context.websocket also carries inferred topics. Local receive takes topic/scope/onMessage and returns a Result containing unsubscribe(). Trusted backend sends are not subjected to remote-client publishing policy; their schemas are still validated. Local listeners are instance-local, and one failed listener does not fail all other listeners.

Emit after a successful commit. Send success means accepted for live delivery, not that all subscribers processed it. A later send failure does not roll back committed data.

## Dedicated socket client [#dedicated-socket-client]

```ts
import { createNileSocketClient } from "@nilejs/client";
import type { Topics } from "./contracts";

type Actions = {
  payments: { "get-status": { paymentId: string } };
};

const socket = createNileSocketClient<Actions, Topics>({
  baseUrl: "https://api.example.com",
  auth: () => ({ token: session.token }),
});

const received = await socket.receive({
  topic: "payments.updated",
  scope: { organizationId },
  onMessage: (message) => renderStatus(message.data.status),
});
if (received.isErr) {
  console.error(received.error);
  return;
}

const statusResult = await socket.invoke({
  service: "payments",
  action: "get-status",
  payload: { paymentId },
});
if (statusResult.isErr) {
  console.error(statusResult.error, statusResult.details);
  return;
}

const sent = await socket.send({
  topic: "payments.updated",
  scope: { organizationId },
  data: { paymentId, status: "paid" },
});
if (sent.isErr) {
  console.error(sent.error);
  return;
}

const unsubscribed = await received.value.unsubscribe();
if (unsubscribed.isErr) {
  console.error(unsubscribed.error);
}
socket.close();
```

Every socket client method returns the same Result as the HTTP client: check `isErr`, then read `value`, or `error` and `details` on failure. The first type parameter is the service/action payload map; the second is the topic contract map. Contracts can be shared, generated or defined independently on the frontend. A manually defined topic member uses { data: Payload, input?: PublishInput, scope?: Scope }; when input is omitted, publishing uses data. Backend InferTopics preserves transformed input/output automatically. Topic scope and publishing input must match the backend wire contract.

receive registers a continuing listener, rather than resolving with the first message. Its Result acknowledges registration. Multiple local listeners can share a server subscription; unsubscribing one keeps the others. On reconnect the client resubscribes and reauthorizes; onSubscriptionError can report failed rejoining. Action calls and messages are not automatically retried or stored for offline delivery. Calls have a finite acknowledgement timeout, which cannot prove a timed-out write did not commit.

The client loads socket.io-client on use. Existing createNileClient remains the HTTP client. No transport or socket argument is passed per invocation. Browser-relative URLs resolve through Socket.IO's browser origin behavior; backend callers need an absolute URL.

## Runtime setup and limits [#runtime-setup-and-limits]

```ts
if (!server.websocket?.bun) {
  throw new Error("Bun socket adapter unavailable");
}
const listener = Bun.serve({
  fetch: server.fetch,
  websocket: server.websocket.bun,
  idleTimeout: server.websocket.idleTimeout,
});
server.lifecycle.register({ name: "listener", close: () => listener.stop(true) });
```

Node applications select runtime: "node" and attach await server.websocket.attachNode(existingHttpServer). Socket detachment/shutdown preserves the application-owned HTTP listener. The app is responsible for closing that listener when desired. Do not attach one adapter to several listeners. Existing Hono-compatible HTTP apps remain supported.

The default Socket.IO path is /socket.io. Set websocket.path and the client's path together to customize it. Browser origins must be explicitly allowed; an absent Origin for backend clients is not authentication. Limits default to 1000 connections, 5s authentication, 1MiB message/buffer bounds, 32 concurrent operations per connection, 100 subscriptions per connection and 600 operations/minute. Customize through maxConnections, authenticationTimeoutMs, maxMessageBytes, maxBufferedBytes, maxConcurrentMessages, maxSubscriptions and messagesPerMinute. Slow clients are disconnected. Socket operations participate in lifecycle admission/draining.

Delivery and subscription state are process-local. A cross-replica adapter bridge and durable event persistence are not supplied. This implementation uses scoped local fanout behind Socket.IO, rather than exposing raw room names or an adapter configuration surface. There is no race-free snapshot/replay protocol: applications needing that must design cursor/snapshot semantics explicitly.

## Export contracts or retrieve them over HTTP [#export-contracts-or-retrieve-them-over-http]

```ts
const schemas = await server.schema();
const written = await server.schema({ path: "./contracts/nile.schemas.json" });
```

Returns a Result with { services, topics }. The destination directory must already exist. File output is a JSON Schema document, not executable TypeScript; it does not preserve arbitrary refinements/transforms as frontend runtime code. Conversion is on demand, and topic conversions are cached by schema identity.

Existing action discovery is unchanged. To retrieve topic schemas through POST /api/services, use:

```json
{"intent":"schema","service":"*","action":"*","payload":{"kind":"topics"}}
```

The existing REST discovery enabled/secret checks apply before conversion or disclosure. No new public unauthenticated discovery route is introduced.


---

# Shared backend utilities

Nile keeps these helpers functional and independent of application models, payment providers or deployment configuration. Use the named `utils` export from `@nilejs/nile`. Framework entry points such as `createNileServer`, service/action factories and server configuration stay at the package root. Existing direct helper imports remain supported.

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";
```

| Use | Helpers |
| --- | --- |
| Database access | `createModel`, `createTransactionVariant`, `getZodSchema`, `dbTry` |
| Failure diagnostics | `handleError`, `describeError` |
| Execution controls | `createQueue`, `createGroupedControl`, `createControlResource`, `createDebounce`, `createThrottle`, `createBatch`, `createRateLimiter` |
| Retry and storage | `retryFnWithJitter`, `createMemoryStore` |
| Client identity | `normalizeIp`, `resolveClientAddress`, `resolveClientIdentity` |

Call each helper through `utils`. Import option and result types as named exports from the package root.

## Safe database failures [#safe-database-failures]

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";

const loaded = await utils.dbTry(() => db.select().from(orders), {
  message: "Could not load orders",
  atFunction: "orders.list",
});

if (loaded.isErr) {
  return loaded;
}
```

Thrown database errors become a safe caller-facing Result. When logging succeeds, its validated log reference is included, following Nile’s existing handleError convention. Model error logs retain that reference so the diagnostic record can be found even outside a request scope. The active Nile logger receives bounded cause metadata, including driver error codes, constraints, tables and routines. An explicit `logger` overrides the current context; standalone use can omit logging. Nile's `createModel` query operations use this wrapper too. Transaction ownership, commit and rollback behavior are unchanged.

Automatic diagnostics omit messages, SQL, parameters, detail and stack traces. `includeMessages: true` explicitly enables bounded error messages for internal diagnosis; driver messages may contain application data, so choose it deliberately. Known Drizzle `Failed query:` wrappers are replaced with a generic summary even in that mode. Supplied custom public messages must be safe for callers.

Returned failures are sanitized too, and successful nested Slang Results are resolved recursively. Logger failure does not replace the operation's safe failure. Reporting follows the synchronous Nile logger contract.

To inspect an error directly:

```ts
const diagnostic = await utils.describeError(error, {
  maxDepth: 5,
  maxFieldLength: 512,
  includeMessages: true,
});
```

Causes appear deepest first. Circular causes, hostile properties and thenable causes are handled without following them indefinitely. Configuration mistakes throw. This helper does not create a separate log viewer or classify business failures automatically.

## Explicit retries and polling [#explicit-retries-and-polling]

```ts
import { utils } from "@nilejs/nile";

const delivered = await utils.retryFnWithJitter({
  fn: (signal) => checkDeliveryStatus({ reference, signal }),
  signal: context.execution?.signal,
  maxAttempts: 8,
  timeoutMs: 60_000,
  baseDelayMs: 1000,
  maxDelayMs: 10_000,
  jitterMs: 500,
  onResult: ({ result, retry, end, stop }) => {
    if (result.isErr) {
      return retry();
    }
    if (result.value.state === "delivered") {
      return end(result.value);
    }
    if (result.value.state === "failed") {
      return stop("Delivery failed");
    }
    return retry();
  },
});

if (delivered.isErr) {
  return delivered;
}
```

Each additional attempt requires the application's explicit decision. `end(value)` returns success; `stop(message)` returns failure; reaching the attempt bound returns a string failure, without pretending it has an arbitrary application error type. Policy exceptions return a safe policy failure. Do not retry a business write unless its idempotency makes repetition appropriate.

Slang `superPromise` supplies the whole-run cooperative deadline and cancellable wait settlement. The first attempt starts immediately unless `initialDelayMs` is provided. Later attempts use exponential backoff, with jitter below the computed cap; the complete delay never exceeds `maxDelayMs`. There is at least a 1ms wait between retries so immediate failures cannot starve cancellation timers.

Defaults: 10 total attempts, 60s whole-run deadline, 2s base delay, 30s delay cap, 500ms jitter and a 20-record metadata history. `maxHistory` can be at most 1000. The policy receives `attempt`, the current Result and bounded `attempts` timing/outcome metadata. Previous payloads/errors are not retained automatically. `startedAt` uses epoch milliseconds by default; `clock` and `random` are injectable for deterministic checks.

Cancellation ends a backoff wait immediately and prevents another attempt. During in-flight work it is cooperative: if a function ignores its signal, the helper awaits actual settlement. This preserves queue concurrency accounting and never starts overlapping attempts. A deadline cannot force JavaScript or a database driver to stop. Queues and lifecycle drain can therefore still observe work that ignores cancellation.

## Bounded ephemeral storage [#bounded-ephemeral-storage]

```ts
const cache = utils.createMemoryStore<OrderSummary>({
  maxKeys: 1000,
  ttlMs: 30_000,
  eviction: "lru",
});

const stored = cache.set({ key: order.id, value: order });
if (stored.isErr) {
  return stored;
}

const cached = cache.get(order.id);
cache.delete(order.id);
```

Default admission is `reject-new`; LRU must be selected deliberately. LRU reads promote entries, while TTL is measured from the most recent set, not the most recent read. An indexed expiry queue keeps one node per expiring key: updates and deletes do not accumulate stale expiry records. Expiration is lazy, without a background timer or whole-store scan on each lookup. Capacity checks and size inspection remove due entries; reads reject an expired target immediately.

There are at most 1000 keys by default. Omit TTL for bounded values that live until removed. Each set can override the configured TTL with a positive millisecond duration. A rejected insertion preserves current live values. Values are held by reference; `has` distinguishes a stored undefined from a miss.

For one-time values:

```ts
const tokens = utils.createMemoryStore<string>({ maxKeys: 1000, ttlMs: 60_000 });
tokens.set({ key: tokenId, value: expectedToken });

const accepted = tokens.consume({ key: tokenId, expected: suppliedToken });
```

Consume is a synchronous compare-and-delete: only the matching caller consumes it. Comparison uses `Object.is`, including reference identity for objects. This is process-local, not a distributed atomic store. `clear()` empties it; `close()` also prevents future writes. Do not use LRU cache eviction for active quota records or durable idempotency claims.

## Reclaim idle keyed queues [#reclaim-idle-keyed-queues]

```ts
const writes = utils.createGroupedControl({
  key: (input: SaveDraft) => input.documentId,
  maxKeys: 1000,
  idleMs: 30_000,
  create: () => utils.createQueue({
    task: saveDraft,
    concurrency: 1,
    capacity: 50,
  }),
});

const result = await writes.run(draft, { signal: signal });
server.lifecycle.register(utils.createControlResource("draft-writes", writes));
```

Each key serializes independently. After real work becomes idle, the timer starts; a later call cancels that timer. A cancelled caller does not make still-running work idle. Idle controls are closed and their keys released, allowing capacity to be reused.

Idle cleanup requires passive `whenIdle()` support, supplied by queues. A control whose drain flushes buffered work, such as a throttle, is rejected for this option. With `idleMs` omitted, existing retention behavior remains unchanged. This protects control timing instead of silently resetting it. Serialization is process-local; database constraints/locks remain application decisions.

## Client address normalization and trust metadata [#client-address-normalization-and-trust-metadata]

```ts
const identity = utils.resolveClientIdentity(request, {
  getClientAddress: (request) => listener.requestIP(request)?.address,
  trustProxy: (address) => config.trustedProxies.includes(address),
});

logger.info({
  atFunction: "requestIdentity",
  message: "Client address resolved",
  data: identity,
});
```

The result includes `address`, listener `peer` and source: `peer`, `forwarded` or `unknown`. IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses normalize to dotted IPv4. Trust checks accept the normalized form and preserve explicit trust in the original spelling. Forwarded addresses are used only when an actual peer and explicit trust permit walking the chain; a header alone never establishes identity.

The existing `resolveClientAddress(request, options)` continues returning just the address. `normalizeIp(value)` is also available separately. The HTTP boundary uses the same resolver for execution client keys. No application config imports, fraud policy, bans or DB audit writes are built into this utility.

## Verification [#verification]

The utility tests use deterministic clocks/cancellation and mock failures. The real DB fixture uses an explicitly approved disposable PGlite database under /tmp, closes it and exercises Drizzle model failures without application configuration. Run it from packages/nile in the source checkout:

```sh
bun test ./scripts/verify-db-utilities.spec.ts
```

## See also [#see-also]

- [Model helpers](/guide/internals/db/create-model)
- [Production operations](/guide/reference/operations)
- [Logging](/guide/internals/logging)

# Application structure

A small team should be able to open an unfamiliar feature and follow it. Use domains to give that work a home, services to list its public operations, and ordinary functions for the business rules behind them.

Register services and actions explicitly. At startup, Nile checks the source structure once and reports misplaced or oversized action files, helping the team keep the same conventions as the application grows.

## Start with one domain [#start-with-one-domain]

```text
src/
  index.ts
  config.ts
  services/
    services.config.ts
    projects/
      index.ts
      actions/
        create-project.ts
        archive-project/
          archive-project.ts
          index.ts
          modules/
            check-archive-policy.ts
      modules/
        types.ts
  business/
    projects/
      calculate-project-progress.ts
  db/
    client.ts
    models/
      projects.ts
  hooks/
    authorize-action.ts
  generated/
    schemas.ts
    types.ts
```

Keep the same domain names across the frontend operation, service, action and model. A teammate looking for project creation can follow `projects.create` to `actions/create-project.ts`, then to the project model. A coding agent has the same explicit registration map and named modules to follow.

For a smaller project, keep the business functions and model inside the domain directory instead. Pick one convention and apply it consistently. The CLI template uses `src/services/services.config.ts` as its registry.

## Grow an action into a folder [#grow-an-action-into-a-folder]

Start a small operation at `service/actions/create-project.ts`. When it needs several private helpers, use `service/actions/create-project/create-project.ts`, export it from `index.ts` and keep its helpers under `modules/`. Code shared by several actions belongs in the service's `modules/` directory.

```sh
bunx @nilejs/cli generate action projects archive --folder
```

Configure `project: { root: ".", structure: "error" }` on the server to fail startup when the structure check finds an error. Existing applications default to `"warn"`; `false` disables checking. In a monorepo, set `root` to the backend package. Source-less bundles skip the check unless a root is explicit. Action entry points above 400 lines receive refactoring guidance.

## Give each layer one job [#give-each-layer-one-job]

| Place | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Action | Describe the operation, validate input, check identity or policy, coordinate the business call and return a Result. |
| Ordinary business function | Calculate or enforce a domain rule that can be reused without an HTTP request. |
| Model or repository | Own the application's data access and return useful success or failure information. |
| Service registry | Show which named operations the application exposes. |
| Shared context | Supply long-lived resources such as a logger or database client. |
| Hook | Apply a common policy or transformation at a defined pipeline point. |

An action does not need a model if it has no persistence. A helper does not need to become an action merely to be reused. For example, both `tickets.complete` and `collaboration.confirm` can call an ordinary scoring function.

## Register the domain explicitly [#register-the-domain-explicitly]

```ts
// services/projects/index.ts
import { createService } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { createProject } from "./actions/create-project";
import { archiveProject } from "./actions/archive-project";

export const projectsService = createService({
  name: "projects",
  description: "Create and manage team projects",
  actions: [createProject, archiveProject],
});
```

```ts
// services/services.config.ts
import { createServices } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { projectsService } from "./projects";

export const services = createServices([projectsService]);
```

Service names must be unique, and action names must be unique within their service. Nile rejects duplicate registration at startup.

## Follow a change through the application [#follow-a-change-through-the-application]

To add project archiving:

1. Find the `projects` service and read a neighboring action.
2. Define the archive input schema beside `actions/archive-project/archive-project.ts`.
3. Check the caller's access before changing project state.
4. Put data access in the project model and reusable domain rules in ordinary functions.
5. Return an explicit Result for success and expected failures.
6. Register the action, then call `projects.archive` from the client.

Keep database selection, migrations and transactions in your application. Nile offers optional [Drizzle model helpers](/guide/internals/db/), but does not require them or manage your schema lifecycle.

## Grow the application without changing the mental model [#grow-the-application-without-changing-the-mental-model]

The maintainer's fintech backend has over 500 actions and continues to grow. The in-house Back Office tool was shipped in days; the reviewed version had 15 services and 78 actions. These are examples of a small team applying the same organization repeatedly, not guarantees about delivery time or request capacity.

The useful constraint is consistency: once someone understands one operation, the next operation has a familiar place to start.

Next: [share dependencies through context](/guide/basics/context), [handle failures consistently](/guide/basics/errors-and-results), and [reuse access policies](/guide/basics/auth).


---

# Deployment

Nile builds a request handler; your runtime starts and owns the listener. A long-running Bun or Node.js service is the straightforward deployment model.

## Choose the adapter explicitly [#choose-the-adapter-explicitly]

- **Bun native:** `runtime: "bun", native: true`, then `Bun.serve({ fetch: server.nativeRest.fetch, port })` after checking it exists.
- **Bun with Hono:** `runtime: "bun"`, omit `native`, then serve `server.rest.app.fetch`.
- **Node.js with Hono:** `runtime: "node"`, omit `native`, then pass `server.rest.app.fetch` to `serve` from `@hono/node-server`.

See [complete startup examples](/guide/start/runtime-adapters). Use a current supported runtime and verify it against your pinned Nile release and dependencies. The recorded performance run used Bun 1.4.2; this is measurement provenance, not a minimum-version guarantee.

## Keep the runtime patched [#keep-the-runtime-patched]

A Nile Js server runs inside your Bun or Node.js process, so every runtime security release applies to it. When one ships, update the runtime, rebuild your container images and restart every process.

- **Node.js:** the October 21, 2026 security release fixed ten vulnerabilities. They include a high-severity Brotli decoder flaw that permits remote code execution, two TLS certificate hostname bypasses and a `dns.resolve` NUL truncation issue. Run at least 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1. `@nilejs/nile` declares these versions in its `engines` field, so npm warns when you install it on an older Node.js. Node.js 20 and older are end-of-life and receive no fixes.
- **Bun:** follow Bun's releases and upgrade with `bun upgrade`. The CLI starter's Dockerfile uses `oven/bun:1-alpine`, so rebuilding the image picks up the newest Bun 1.x release.
- **Decompression:** Nile Js does not decompress request bodies. If you add decompression middleware, or your code calls `fetch` on servers you do not control, compressed data from outside is decoded inside your process. Keep the runtime patched and keep request size limits in place.

Check the running version with `node -v` or `bun -v`, in the same image or host that serves production traffic.

## Prepare production configuration [#prepare-production-configuration]

Keep application settings in your own configuration module and supply them to the server. Before deployment:

1. Limit `allowedOrigins` to the frontends that need access. CORS is not authorization.
2. Configure authentication and enforce action-level access policies.
3. Leave discovery disabled unless you need it; protect enabled discovery with an appropriate secret and network policy.
4. Configure upload limits and static assets only where needed.
5. Supply a logger and decide where its files or output will live.
6. Select a rate-limit store appropriate to the number of running instances. An in-memory limit is per process.

Do not place production credentials in checked-in examples or browser bundles.

## Own the process lifecycle [#own-the-process-lifecycle]

Run the listener under your hosting platform, container supervisor or service manager. Set its host and port through application configuration, terminate TLS at your chosen boundary, and implement graceful shutdown for the listener and application-owned resources.

`rest.enableStatus: true` adds `GET /status` and `GET /ready` at the root of the server, outside your API prefix. Readiness follows Nile’s lifecycle state. Register application-owned resources with `server.lifecycle`, and connect the deployment shutdown signal to `server.lifecycle.shutdown()` before closing the listener. See [lifecycle and shutdown](/guide/reference/operations#deploy-and-shut-down-predictably).

Nile prints startup service/action registration stats by default. `logServices: false` turns off that output; `server.stats()` returns the startup snapshot either way. Registration timing is not ongoing request latency or a full profiler.

## Keep persistence and scale decisions explicit [#keep-persistence-and-scale-decisions-explicit]

Nile does not require a database or run a schema migration for you. The CLI template's PGLite startup setup is an example application choice. Configure persistent storage, backups, migrations and transaction boundaries for your own data layer before production use.

For multiple instances, shared state, sessions, jobs and external resources need an application-level plan. The consistent service/action structure helps the team maintain a growing codebase; it is not automatic distributed infrastructure.

Serverless or edge deployment needs a separate compatibility and lifecycle review. Do not assume every Hono target works with Nile's filesystem, AsyncLocalStorage and application dependencies.


---

# From REST to Nile

A growing product adds operations such as approving a submission, archiving a project or refunding a payment. Nile names those operations directly: `projects.archive`, `submissions.approve`, `payments.refund`.

The goal is a consistent place for the team to work. You still design the operation, its input and its access policy. Nile gives it a common invocation shape rather than another per-operation route.

## One interface, named operations [#one-interface-named-operations]

```json
{
  "intent": "execute",
  "service": "projects",
  "action": "archive",
  "payload": { "projectId": "project-123" }
}
```

Send this to `POST /api/services` when `rest.baseUrl` is `/api`.

| Familiar HTTP concept | Nile application concept |
|---|---|
| A domain route group | A service such as `projects` |
| An operation handler | A named action such as `archive` |
| Path, query or body input | Action payload checked with a Zod schema |
| A common access policy | A global or action hook |
| A frontend request helper | `client.invoke({ service, action, payload })` |

Business logic can stay in ordinary functions and data access can stay in your chosen models. See [application structure](/guide/start/application-structure).

## What the constraint buys a small team [#what-the-constraint-buys-a-small-team]

Every operation has the same places to look for validation, policy and result handling. A new teammate can follow one action and use that pattern again. The frontend calls the business operation by name, while the registry provides a map of the application's capabilities.

Nile precomputes action lookups at startup. That avoids scanning the action list on each call; it does not by itself guarantee higher HTTP throughput than another router. See the [measured workload](/guide/reference/performance).

## Keep HTTP where it is useful [#keep-http-where-it-is-useful]

Webhooks, authentication callbacks and streaming responses can use [custom routes](/guide/basics/custom-routes). Choose native or Hono APIs for the selected adapter.

The shared POST endpoint has trade-offs. Standard GET caching does not automatically apply to actions. Existing REST gateways, per-route analytics and generated OpenAPI integrations may need adaptation. Runtime `explore` and `schema` can describe registered operations when [discovery is enabled](/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents); they are not an OpenAPI server or a complete replacement for application documentation.

Move an existing application [one domain at a time](/guide/start/migration).


---

# Getting started

This walkthrough creates a Nile Js project, runs it and calls its starter action with curl. Then you add an action that changes data and call it from a small TypeScript client. Each step says what you should see when it worked.

Nile Js uses Bun's native HTTP server. The starter stores its data in an embedded PGlite database, so you do not install or run a database server.

## Check the prerequisites [#check-the-prerequisites]

1. Install [Bun](https://bun.sh). Check the version:

```sh
bun --version
```

You should see `1.4.2` or a later 1.4 release. This guide was verified with Bun 1.4.2. Older versions were not tested.

2. Check that curl is available:

```sh
curl --version
```

You should see a first line that starts with `curl`.

## Create the project [#create-the-project]

```sh
bunx @nilejs/cli new my-app
cd my-app
```

You should see `Created my-app` and a short list of next commands. The command copies the starter files. It does not install packages yet.

## Install the packages [#install-the-packages]

```sh
bun install
grep '"version"' node_modules/@nilejs/nile/package.json
```

You should see `"version": "1.0.0",`. If the version is older, stop here and read the last troubleshooting item on this page.

## Look at what you got [#look-at-what-you-got]

The starter has this structure. The comments describe what each file is for.

```text
my-app/
├── .dockerignore              Files left out of the Docker build
├── .env.example               Environment variable template (no variables yet)
├── .gitignore                 Keeps node_modules, .env, data and logs out of git
├── Dockerfile                 Container build (not covered in this guide)
├── docker-compose.yml         Compose file (not covered in this guide)
├── docker-compose.dev.yml     Development compose file (not covered in this guide)
├── drizzle.config.ts          Drizzle Kit settings for database migrations
├── package.json               Scripts and dependencies
├── README.md                  Project notes and request examples
├── tsconfig.json              TypeScript settings, including the @/ import alias
└── src/
    ├── index.ts               Server entry point: Nile setup, port and logger
    ├── db/
    │   ├── client.ts          PGlite database and Drizzle client
    │   ├── index.ts           Barrel export for database code
    │   ├── schema.ts          The tasks table definition
    │   ├── types.ts           Task and NewTask types
    │   └── models/
    │       ├── index.ts       Barrel export for models
    │       └── tasks.ts       taskModel with create, find, update and delete helpers
    └── services/
        ├── services.config.ts Registry of services and their actions
        └── tasks/actions/
            ├── create.ts      tasks.create
            ├── list.ts        tasks.list
            ├── get.ts         tasks.get
            ├── update.ts      tasks.update
            └── delete.ts      tasks.delete
```

`bun install` also creates `node_modules/` and `bun.lock`. Running the server creates a `data/` folder for the database. The starter's `.gitignore` already keeps `node_modules/`, `.env` and `data/` out of git.

## Start the server [#start-the-server]

```sh
cp .env.example .env
bun run dev
```

The `.env` file only contains a comment for now. Keep it so that later variables have a home.

You should see a table with the `tasks` service and five actions, then the startup lines. The timing numbers vary:

```text
Registered 1 service and 5 actions in 0.2ms
00:35:06.275 INFO  onBoot my-app booted - PGLite schema ready
Booted in 13650.2ms
my-app server ready in 13.7s
my-app listening on http://localhost:8000
```

The first start can take between 10 and 30 seconds because PGlite creates the `data/` folder. Later starts are faster. Wait for the `listening` line before you send requests. Keep this terminal open. Press Ctrl+C to stop the server.

## Make your first request [#make-your-first-request]

Open a second terminal in the `my-app` folder and run:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"intent":"execute","service":"tasks","action":"create","payload":{"title":"My first task"}}'
```

You should see a JSON response with `"status": true`. The `id`, `created_at` and `updated_at` values change on every run:

```json
{
  "status": true,
  "message": "Action 'tasks.create' executed",
  "data": {
    "task": {
      "id": "9b4be379-a2e5-4edb-b7df-8654536b629d",
      "title": "My first task",
      "description": "",
      "status": "pending",
      "created_at": "2026-10-21T00:26:46.342Z",
      "updated_at": "2026-10-21T00:26:46.342Z"
    }
  }
}
```

Copy the `id` value. You need it in the next section.

Now send a payload that fails validation:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"intent":"execute","service":"tasks","action":"create","payload":{"title":""}}'
```

You should see `"status": false`, a message that names the field and one entry per failed field in `data.issues`:

```json
{
  "status": false,
  "message": "Validation failed: ✖ Title is required\n  → at title",
  "data": {
    "issues": [{ "path": "title", "message": "Title is required" }]
  }
}
```

Every request goes to `POST /api/services`. The `intent` field selects the operation: `execute` runs an action, `explore` lists services and actions, and `schema` returns an action's input schema.

## Add an action that changes data [#add-an-action-that-changes-data]

You will add `tasks.complete`. It marks one task as `done` and returns the saved task.

### Generate the action file [#generate-the-action-file]

```sh
bun run gen action tasks complete
```

You should see `Action created at src/services/tasks/actions/complete.ts` and a hint to import `completeAction`. The generator does not change `services.config.ts`; you register the action yourself in the next step.

### Replace the generated code [#replace-the-generated-code]

Open `src/services/tasks/actions/complete.ts` and replace its contents with this file:

```ts
import { createAction } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { Err, Ok } from "slang-ts";
import { z } from "zod";
import { taskModel } from "@/db/models";

const completeTaskSchema = z.object({
  id: z.uuid(),
});

type CompleteTaskInput = z.infer<typeof completeTaskSchema>;

const completeTaskHandler = async (input: CompleteTaskInput) => {
  const result = await taskModel.update({
    id: input.id,
    data: { status: "done" },
  });

  if (result.isErr) {
    return Err(result.error);
  }

  return Ok({ task: result.value });
};

export const completeAction = createAction<CompleteTaskInput>({
  name: "complete",
  description: "Mark a task as done",
  validation: completeTaskSchema,
  handler: completeTaskHandler,
});
```

The schema checks the input before the handler runs. The handler returns `Ok` with the saved task or `Err` with a message. The Results section in [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) explains that pattern.

### Register the action [#register-the-action]

Open `src/services/services.config.ts`, add the import, and add `completeAction` to the `tasks` actions list. The complete file should read:

```ts
import { createServices, type Services } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { completeAction } from "./tasks/actions/complete";
import { createTaskAction } from "./tasks/actions/create";
import { deleteTaskAction } from "./tasks/actions/delete";
import { getTaskAction } from "./tasks/actions/get";
import { listTaskAction } from "./tasks/actions/list";
import { updateTaskAction } from "./tasks/actions/update";

export const services: Services = createServices([
  {
    name: "tasks",
    description: "Task management with CRUD operations",
    meta: { version: "1.0.0" },
    actions: [
      createTaskAction,
      listTaskAction,
      getTaskAction,
      updateTaskAction,
      deleteTaskAction,
      completeAction,
    ],
  },
]);
```

### Call it [#call-it]

`bun run dev` watches your files and restarts the server when you save. Wait for the `listening` line to appear again in the server terminal.

Replace `PASTE_TASK_ID` with the `id` from your first request:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/services \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"intent":"execute","service":"tasks","action":"complete","payload":{"id":"PASTE_TASK_ID"}}'
```

You should see `"status": true` and the task with `"status": "done"`.

## Call the action from a client [#call-the-action-from-a-client]

`@nilejs/client` is a small typed client for Nile Js. It works in a browser app and in server-side TypeScript. In your project folder, install it:

```sh
bun add @nilejs/client
```

Create `client-check.ts` in the project root, next to `package.json`:

```ts
import { createNileClient } from "@nilejs/client";
import { z } from "zod";

interface ServicePayloads {
  tasks: {
    create: { title: string };
    complete: { id: string };
  };
}

const createdTaskSchema = z.object({
  task: z.object({
    id: z.string(),
    status: z.string(),
  }),
});

const nile = createNileClient<ServicePayloads>({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:8000/api",
});

const runClientCheck = async (): Promise<void> => {
  const created = await nile.invoke({
    service: "tasks",
    action: "create",
    payload: { title: "Written from the client" },
  });

  if (created.isErr) {
    console.error(created.error);
    return;
  }

  const createdTask = createdTaskSchema.parse(created.value);

  const completed = await nile.invoke({
    service: "tasks",
    action: "complete",
    payload: { id: createdTask.task.id },
  });

  if (completed.isErr) {
    console.error(completed.error);
    return;
  }

  console.log("created", createdTask.task.id, createdTask.task.status);
  console.log("completed", JSON.stringify(completed.value));
};

await runClientCheck();
```

With the server still running, run the file in your second terminal:

```sh
bun run client-check.ts
```

You should see one line for the created task (with `pending`) and one line for the completed task with `"status":"done"`. Every client method returns a Result, the same pattern the server uses. Check `isErr` first, then read `value` on success or `error` on failure.

A browser app that runs on another origin, such as `http://localhost:5173`, must be listed in `rest.allowedOrigins` in `src/index.ts`:

```ts
  rest: {
    baseUrl: "/api",
    host: "localhost",
    port: 8000,
    allowedOrigins: ["http://localhost:8000", "http://localhost:5173"],
    enableStatus: true,
    discovery: { enabled: true },
  },
```

Without the origin, the server does not send an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, and the browser blocks the response. The server restarts by itself when you save this file.

## Check the status endpoints [#check-the-status-endpoints]

`enableStatus: true` adds two `GET` endpoints at the root of the server, outside `/api`:

```sh
curl -s http://localhost:8000/status
curl -s http://localhost:8000/ready
```

You should see `{"status":true,"message":"my-app is running","data":{}}` from `/status` and `{"status":true,"message":"Ready","data":{}}` from `/ready`. Use `/ready` to check that the server finished booting. Use `/status` for a simple liveness check.

## What to read next [#what-to-read-next]

- [Application structure](/guide/start/application-structure) explains how to group services and actions as the project grows.
- [Services](/guide/basics/services) and [actions](/guide/basics/actions) describe the registration and definition rules.
- [Frontend client](/guide/basics/client) covers errors, request options and generated input types.
- [Errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results) explains the three response shapes.
- [Runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) explains how to move an existing Hono application.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

- **`curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 8000`.** The server has not finished booting, or it stopped. Wait for the `listening` line. If the server exited, read the error printed just above the prompt.

- **`Failed to start server. Is port 8000 in use?`** Another process is using port 8000. Stop that process and start `bun run dev` again. To use a different port, change `port` in the `rest` block of `src/index.ts`, then update the URLs in your requests and in `baseUrl`.

- **`Route not found. Use POST /api/services for all operations.` with HTTP 404.** The request used the wrong method or path. Operations use `POST /api/services`. Only `/status` and `/ready` use `GET` at the root.

- **`Action 'complete' not found in service 'tasks'`.** The server does not know the action yet. Check that `completeAction` is imported and listed in the `actions` list in `services.config.ts`, then save the file. `bun run dev` restarts the server when you save.

- **A new action is missing after you edit a file.** Check that the server terminal printed the `listening` line again after you saved. If you started the server with `bun run src/index.ts` instead of `bun run dev`, it does not watch files; stop it and run `bun run dev`.

- **`Could not auto-register. Add manually:`** This message appears after `generate service` when `services.config.ts` no longer ends with the services list, for example after you reorganized it. Copy the printed import and the service entry into that file yourself.

- **`Group action entry points under actions/` at startup.** The server stops before it listens. A file was placed directly in a service folder, such as `src/services/documents/inspect.ts`. Move it to `src/services/documents/actions/inspect.ts` and update its import in `services.config.ts`. The CLI already creates the `actions/` folder.

- **`Dependencies not installed.`** The CLI generators stop when `node_modules` is missing. Run `bun install` in the project root, then run the generator again.

- **The browser prints `No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header`.** Add the page's origin to `rest.allowedOrigins` and save the file. See [Call the action from a client](#call-the-action-from-a-client).

- **`Validation failed` in the response.** The request reached the action, and its input did not match the schema. Read the field named after `→ at`, correct the payload and send the request again.

- **TypeScript reports that two `Result` types are not compatible.** Two copies of `slang-ts` are installed. Run `bun pm ls | grep slang-ts`; if you see more than one version, run `bun add slang-ts@0.0.9` so your code and Nile Js share one copy.

- **`@nilejs/nile` shows a version older than `1.0.0`.** This guide documents Nile Js 1.0.0. Earlier releases have a different starter and different commands. Install the 1.0.0 release, then start again from `bunx @nilejs/cli new`.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters)
- [HTTP interaction](/guide/basics/interacting)
- [Deployment](/guide/start/deploy)

# Migration guide

Start with an operation your team understands. Keep its business logic and data layer, give it a Nile action boundary, and verify its existing behavior before moving more traffic.

## Map the operation [#map-the-operation]

| Existing API | Nile operation |
|---|---|
| `POST /projects` | `projects.create` |
| `GET /projects/:id` | `projects.get` with `{ projectId }` |
| `POST /projects/:id/archive` | `projects.archive` with `{ projectId }` |

The client must switch to `POST /api/services` with the service/action envelope. Simply forwarding an old path to Nile does not translate its parameters or request body. If existing clients must keep their URLs, write an explicit compatibility route or retain the old handler during migration.

## Keep the business function [#keep-the-business-function]

This action adapts an existing application function that already returns a Result:

```ts
import { createAction } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { z } from "zod";
import { archiveProject } from "../../business/projects/archive-project";

const archiveProjectSchema = z.object({
  projectId: z.string().min(1),
});

type ArchiveProjectInput = z.infer<typeof archiveProjectSchema>;

const archiveProjectHandler = (input: ArchiveProjectInput) => {
  return archiveProject(input);
};

export const archiveProjectAction = createAction<ArchiveProjectInput>({
  name: "archive",
  description: "Archive a project",
  validation: archiveProjectSchema,
  handler: archiveProjectHandler,
});
```

Register it under the projects service. Preserve the original authorization rules; the short example above does not add an access policy.

## Make failure paths explicit [#make-failure-paths-explicit]

Map ordinary business failures to `Err(message)` and success to `Ok(data)`. Wrap potentially failing external operations in `safeTry` and decide which message is safe to return. Nile action failures normally map to HTTP 400, including an action-level not-found error; they do not preserve arbitrary status codes from the previous API.

Keep HTTP-specific status behavior in a custom route when consumers depend on it. See [errors and Results](/guide/basics/errors-and-results).

## Reuse policies without losing them [#reuse-policies-without-losing-them]

Configure `auth` plus `isProtected` for built-in JWT verification, or enforce your chosen session provider in a global before hook. Implement role and organization checks explicitly. Hooks execute before input validation, so they must not assume the payload has already been validated.

See [authentication and access control](/guide/basics/auth) and [hook ordering](/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines).

## Verify, then move the next operation [#verify-then-move-the-next-operation]

Compare success, invalid input, missing identity, denied access and downstream failure against the existing behavior. Update the frontend call and its error handling. Move traffic only after those contracts are understood; keep a rollback path during the transition.

You can retain existing models, queries and integrations. Database migrations and transactional behavior remain application responsibilities. See [runtime adapters](/guide/start/runtime-adapters) before replacing Hono-specific integrations.


---

# Runtime adapters

Your services, actions, validation and Result handling stay the same across Nile's two HTTP adapters. Choose the adapter for the environment and HTTP integrations your application needs.

| Application | Configuration | HTTP API |
|---|---|---|
| New Bun application | `runtime: "bun", native: true` | `server.nativeRest` |
| Existing Bun/Hono application | `runtime: "bun"`, omit `native` | `server.rest.app` |
| Node.js application | `runtime: "node"`, omit `native` | `server.rest.app` |

Hono remains the default compatibility path. Updating Nile does not opt an existing application into Bun native. Native requires an explicit Bun runtime; a conflicting configuration fails at setup.

## Bun native [#bun-native]

```ts
import { createNileServer } from "@nilejs/nile";
import { services } from "./services/services.config";

const server = await createNileServer({
  serverName: "Team workspace",
  services,
  runtime: "bun",
  native: true,
  rest: { baseUrl: "/api", allowedOrigins: ["http://localhost:3000"] },
});

const native = server.nativeRest;
if (!native) {
  throw new Error("Bun native transport was not initialized");
}
Bun.serve({ port: 8000, fetch: native.fetch });
```

## Hono on Bun or Node.js [#hono-on-bun-or-nodejs]

Use the same server configuration with `native` omitted. For Bun, start the Hono handler with:

```ts
const app = server.rest?.app;
if (!app) {
  throw new Error("Hono transport was not initialized");
}
Bun.serve({ port: 8000, fetch: app.fetch });
```

For Node.js, select `runtime: "node"` when constructing the server, then start its Hono handler with the Node adapter:

```ts
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";

const app = server.rest?.app;
if (!app) {
  throw new Error("Hono transport was not initialized");
}
serve({ port: 8000, fetch: app.fetch });
```

Construction and listening are separate in every case. Runtime support here is Bun and Node.js; do not assume other Hono deployment targets are supported by Nile.

## Move an existing Hono application deliberately [#move-an-existing-hono-application-deliberately]

Changing `native` is only one part of migration. Replace Hono-specific request access, routes, middleware and plugins with native equivalents.

| Hono integration | Bun native equivalent |
|---|---|
| `server.rest.app.get(path, handler)` | `server.nativeRest.route("GET", path, handler)` |
| `server.rest.addMiddleware(path, handler)` | `server.nativeRest.addMiddleware(path, handler)` |
| Hono `c.req.raw` | Native `c.request` |
| Hono `c.req.param("id")` | Native `c.params.id` |
| `context.get("rest")` for Hono Context | `context.get<NativeRequestContext>("nativeRest")` |
| `context.getSession("rest")` | Unchanged authenticated-session key |

Native request contexts expose `json`, `text`, `respond`, outgoing `headers`, `setHeader`, request-local `get`/`set`, and cached `parseBody`. Standard Request and Response APIs handle headers, URLs and streams.

Global hooks, local hooks, JWT configuration, multipart actions, discovery, static files, status, rate limiting and startup stats use the same application model. Callback and custom-store types that depend on the HTTP adapter differ. Migrate Hono-context CORS callbacks to `rest.cors.actions` native policies; static boolean and plain-option action CORS settings can remain.

Test authentication, authorization, custom routes, uploads and middleware before switching an existing deployment. See [custom routes](/guide/basics/custom-routes) and [deployment](/guide/start/deploy).
